excerpt_en: Walikale, January 14, 2026 -AFC/M23 rebels launched coordinated attacks on Tuesday afternoon, January 13, targeting the villages of Buma, Mpombi, and Iteya in the Kisimba group, Walikale territory, North Kivu. After nearly three hours of fighting, the attackers were repelled by t
body_en:
Walikale, January 14, 2026 -AFC/M23 rebels launched coordinated attacks on Tuesday afternoon, January 13, targeting the villages of Buma, Mpombi, and Iteya in the Kisimba group, Walikale territory, North Kivu.
After nearly three hours of fighting, the attackers were repelled by the Wazalendo, forcing the rebels to withdraw toward Mpety, in the Banakindi area, according to sources on the ground.
The human toll from the clashes has not yet been established. However, the fighting triggered a mass displacement of residents into surrounding bush areas. Local administrative authorities report that displaced families began gradually returning to their villages on Wednesday.
As of now, Buma, Mpombi, and Iteya remain under Wazalendo control, while the security situation in the area remains fragile.

excerpt_en: Walikale, January 15, 2026 -Nine fighters from the AFC/M23 rebellion surrendered to the Wazalendo of the FPP/AP (Patriotic Forces for Peace/People's Army) on Monday, January 12, 2026, in Fatua, in the Munzoa area (Kisimba group), Walikale territory, North Kivu. According to secur
body_en:
Walikale, January 15, 2026 -Nine fighters from the AFC/M23 rebellion surrendered to the Wazalendo of the FPP/AP (Patriotic Forces for Peace/People's Army) on Monday, January 12, 2026, in Fatua, in the Munzoa area (Kisimba group), Walikale territory, North Kivu.
According to security sources, the fighters came from the Lubero territory and said they were fleeing the suffering they endured within the rebellion.
The fighters surrendered with five weapons. They are reportedly former FARDC soldiers captured during the fall of Goma.
Military authorities, confirming the surrender, called on other compatriots still within rebel ranks to break away and continue to honor their oath to the nation.
The surrendered fighters were handed over by the Wazalendo to the FARDC (Armed Forces of the Democratic Republic of Congo) in Fatua and are reportedly en route to Pinga.

title_en: AFC/M23 Reaches Lemera, Symbolic Village in the Uvira Highlands
excerpt_en: Lemera DRC, January 16, 2026 -Despite calls for a ceasefire between government forces and the AFC/M23 rebellion in North and South Kivu, military operations continue on the ground. In this context, AFC/M23 rebels entered Lemera, in the Bafuliro chiefdom, Uvira territory highlands
body_en:
Lemera DRC, January 16, 2026 -Despite calls for a ceasefire between government forces and the AFC/M23 rebellion in North and South Kivu, military operations continue on the ground. In this context, AFC/M23 rebels entered Lemera, in the Bafuliro chiefdom, Uvira territory highlands, South Kivu, on Thursday, January 15.
Rebel columns were observed early in the morning, following violent clashes with the Wazalendo (local inhabitants) in this strategic village.
According to local sources, the rebels advanced through several villages, including Kaziba, Langala, and Rubanga, to reach Lemera. “The rebels crossed Langala and Rubanga before splitting into two groups. One headed towards Kidote and the other towards Nakandongo,” a civil society source reported. This account is corroborated by multiple sources in the region.
Lemera, located about 30 kilometers from Bwegera, just beyond Luvungi off National Route 5 (RN5), lies along a corridor that passes through Kiringye, Namutiri, Rubanga, Bwesho, and Kidote.
The village holds strong symbolic importance in Uvira territory, as it once hosted the AFDL rebellion’s military training center. For many observers, the capture of Lemera could open the way toward Mulenge and Katala, in the Uvira highlands.
Lemera is also significant for having hosted the original site of Panzi Hospital, where Dr. Denis Mukwege, 2018 Nobel Peace Prize laureate, served as medical director in 1996.

title: AFC/M23 Appeals to the UN and Places the City of Uvira Under the “Full and Complete” Responsibility of the International Community

title_en: AFC/M23 Appeals to the UN and Places the City of Uvira Under the “Full and Complete” Responsibility of the International Community
excerpt_en: Uvira DRC, January 16, 2026 -The AFC/M23 rebellion, which controls large areas of North Kivu and South Kivu, announced that it has placed the strategic city of Uvira under the responsibility of the international community. In a letter dated Thursday, January 15, 2026, to UN Secre
body_en:
Uvira DRC, January 16, 2026 -The AFC/M23 rebellion, which controls large areas of North Kivu and South Kivu, announced that it has placed the strategic city of Uvira under the responsibility of the international community. In a letter dated Thursday, January 15, 2026, to UN Secretary-General António Guterres, the group’s political coordinator, Corneille Nangaa, said the move follows the rebels’ withdrawal decision announced on December 15, 2025, recently reaffirmed, and their stated commitment to the ceasefire.
The Rwandan-backed movement said it is immediately withdrawing its “observation and monitoring unit” and declining all responsibility for security in the city.
“With immediate effect, our organization is withdrawing its observation and monitoring unit, which was preparing the transfer of the city to the neutral force, and is declining all responsibility for the security of this important city in South Kivu province. It is now incumbent upon the international community, within the framework of its responsibilities and commitments, to ensure the protection of civilian populations, the maintenance of peace, and the security of all the inhabitants of Uvira, without discrimination,” wrote Corneille Nangaa.
In the same letter, he warned against threats posed by actors not party to the peace agreements, including the Burundian army, the FDLR, the Wazalendo militias, and mercenaries supporting the FARDC, saying their presence could plunge Uvira into chaos and undermine regional peace efforts led by the African Union, Qatar, the United States, and other partners.
“We solemnly draw the international community’s attention to the fact that the Burundian army, the FDLR, the so-called Wazalendo armed groups, and the mercenaries supporting the FARDC pose a clear threat to the city of Uvira. These armed actors are not party to any commitments arising from a peace process. Therefore, their presence and activities represent a direct and immediate threat not only to the civilian population, but also to the ongoing peace process and to regional stability as a whole,” he stated.
He added:
“In this worrying context, it is essential that the international community fully assume its responsibilities and ensure the rapid deployment of a truly neutral force in the city of Uvira, in order to prevent it from descending once again into chaos, devastation, and violence. This initiative demonstrates our firm commitment to protecting civilians, consolidating the ceasefire, and creating the conditions for a lasting peace based on dialogue, respect for international commitments, and the principles of international humanitarian law.”
This initiative comes at a time when, despite the involvement of US President Donald Trump and the apparent acceleration of the Washington process, illustrated by the ratification of agreements by Presidents Félix Tshisekedi and Paul Kagame, the situation on the ground remains fragile. Kinshasa and Kigali continue to struggle to align positions, amid persistent tensions and mutual accusations of failing to uphold commitments made within ongoing diplomatic initiatives.
The same challenges affect the Doha talks, conducted under the auspices of the Emir of Qatar between Kinshasa and the Rwandan-backed AFC/M23, which have yet to yield tangible results on the ground. These negotiations, intended to complement the Washington agreements by addressing root causes such as the restoration of state authority and the reintegration of armed groups, remain stalled. Several agreed measures - including the joint communiqué, the ceasefire mechanism, the declaration of principles, and the framework agreement - have yet to be implemented.
This diplomatic inertia has fueled the continuation of violent clashes between the AFC/M23 and government forces. In addition, the national dialogue called for by several socio-political actors to support these initiatives has not yet been convened.
After announcing its withdrawal from mediation in March 2025, Angola is gradually and discreetly reintegrating into the process. Luanda has relaunched broad consultations, increasing contacts with nearly all stakeholders. Meanwhile, Togo plans to host a high-level meeting on Saturday, January 17, 2026, aimed at strengthening the coherence and consolidation of peace initiatives in the DRC and the Great Lakes region.
It is in this context that João Lourenço, President of Angola and current Chairperson of the African Union, received representatives of the National Episcopal Conference of Congo (CENCO) and the Church of Christ in Congo (ECC) in Luanda. Discussions focused on the need to establish an inclusive national dialogue, bringing together all Congolese stakeholders to achieve lasting peace in the Democratic Republic of Congo. Participants agreed that this process should be launched without delay.
These consultations form part of broader diplomatic efforts to end the armed conflict in eastern DRC, marked by continued fighting between government forces and the Rwandan-backed AFC/M23, according to the United Nations.

title: In Lubumbashi, Jacquemain Shabani Calls for Constant Vigilance to Contain Security Threats Between the DRC and Zambia
excerpt: Lubumbashi Haut-Katanga, January 16, 2026 - The 14th session of the Joint Defense and Security Commission between the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) and the Republic of Zambia concluded on Thursday, January 15, in Lubumbashi, the capital of Haut-Katanga province. This high-le
title_en: In Lubumbashi, Jacquemain Shabani Calls for Constant Vigilance to Contain Security Threats Between the DRC and Zambia
excerpt_en: Lubumbashi Haut-Katanga, January 16, 2026 - The 14th session of the Joint Defense and Security Commission between the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) and the Republic of Zambia concluded on Thursday, January 15, in Lubumbashi, the capital of Haut-Katanga province. This high-le
body_en:
Lubumbashi Haut-Katanga, January 16, 2026 - The 14th session of the Joint Defense and Security Commission between the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) and the Republic of Zambia concluded on Thursday, January 15, in Lubumbashi, the capital of Haut-Katanga province. This high-level bilateral meeting brought together delegations from both countries over three days to examine shared security challenges in a regional context marked by a resurgence of cross-border threats.
The DRC-Zambia Joint Defense and Security Commission serves as a permanent framework for consultation between the two neighboring states, which share a long border. Its mandate is to strengthen security cooperation, prevent conflicts, combat cross-border crime, and ensure the stability of border areas.
This 14th session took place against a backdrop of persistent security challenges, including armed banditry, transnational crime, terrorism, and border incursions, all of which require close coordination and a concerted response between Kinshasa and Lusaka.
At the close of the session, the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of the Interior, Security, Decentralization, and Customary Affairs of the DRC, Jacquemain Shabani, emphasized the gravity and complexity of these shared threats.
“The discussions highlighted terrorism, transnational crime, banditry, and border violations. It is imperative to maintain constant vigilance and continuously adapt to address them,” Mr. Shabani stated.
He stressed the need to move beyond commitments in principle and called for the effective implementation of the decisions taken.
“I recommend rigorous follow-up to the adopted resolutions so that defense and security issues between our two countries produce the results expected by our respective governments,” he added.
For his part, Jacob Mwimbu, Minister of Home Affairs and Security of Zambia, welcomed the progress made by the Joint Commission and reaffirmed his country’s commitment to strengthening security cooperation with the DRC.
“In the area of defense and security, our Commission has successfully implemented concrete strategies to combat cross-border crime and other offenses that threaten defense and security,” he stated.
He also underscored the close link between security and economic development.
“We recognize that without peace and security, the economic growth objectives of our Commission will be difficult to achieve.”
Emphasizing the importance of collaboration between the security services of both countries, the Zambian minister added:
“Our security services have a duty to maintain their cooperation in defense and security matters. It is therefore crucial for us to strengthen our collaboration and conduct joint security and defense operations.”
He concluded with a clear commitment:
“I reaffirm Zambia’s commitment to ensuring the success of the Commission’s mandate. Zambia remains committed to maintaining peace at the regional, national, and international levels.”
The closing of this 14th session marks a new stage in strengthening security relations between the DRC and Zambia, with both countries reaffirming their commitment to translating adopted resolutions into concrete actions to guarantee the security of their populations and the stability of their shared border areas.

title: Persistent Insecurity Escalates
excerpt: Kibua, Walikale, January 17, 2026 - The security situation remains precarious in Kibua and its surroundings, in the Ihana group (Walikale territory), North Kivu, with several serious incidents reported on Thursday, January 15. According to the head of the Ihana group, Mwami Kitwa
title_en: Persistent Insecurity Escalates
excerpt_en: Kibua, Walikale, January 17, 2026 - The security situation remains precarious in Kibua and its surroundings, in the Ihana group (Walikale territory), North Kivu, with several serious incidents reported on Thursday, January 15. According to the head of the Ihana group, Mwami Kitwa
body_en:
Kibua, Walikale, January 17, 2026 - The security situation remains precarious in Kibua and its surroundings, in the Ihana group (Walikale territory), North Kivu, with several serious incidents reported on Thursday, January 15.
According to the head of the Ihana group, Mwami Kitwana Ngulu Séraphin, the first incident involved a member of the FARDC (Armed Forces of the Democratic Republic of Congo) who was shot in the left foot. The exact circumstances are unclear, but local sources suggest it occurred following a heated argument with superiors.
Later the same day, another FARDC soldier stabbed a young boy in the hand and attempted to shoot him moments later, sparking outrage and fear among residents already traumatized by the recurring insecurity in the region.
The situation worsened further with the intervention of a militiaman from the NDC-Renovated armed group, who carried out armed robberies on Kalonge/Mubea Hill. Vehicles, particularly motorcycle taxis, were looted, temporarily paralyzing traffic and intensifying the sense of insecurity among road users.
In response to this resurgence of violence, Mwami Kitwana Ngulu Séraphin called on military and administrative authorities to take urgent measures to restore order and protect the civilian population.
Meanwhile, the residents of Kibua continue to live in constant fear, urging the State to strengthen discipline within the regular forces and the wazalendo operating in this volatile part of North Kivu.

The exact circumstances are unclear, but local sources suggest it occurred following a heated argument with superiors.

Vehicles, particularly motorcycle taxis, were looted, temporarily paralyzing traffic and intensifying the sense of insecurity among road users.
In response to this resurgence of violence, Mwami Kitwana Ngulu Séraphin called on military and administrative authorities to take urgent measures to restore order and protect the civilian population.
Meanwhile, the residents of Kibua continue to live in constant fear, urging the State to strengthen discipline within the regular forces and the wazalendo operating in this volatile part of North Kivu.

According to the head of the Ihana group, Mwami Kitwana Ngulu Séraphin, the first incident involved a member of the FARDC (Armed Forces of the Democratic Republic of Congo) who was shot in the left foot. The exact circumstances are unclear, but local sources suggest it occurred following a heated argument with superiors.
Later the same day, another FARDC soldier stabbed a young boy in the hand and attempted to shoot him moments later, sparking outrage and fear among residents already traumatized by the recurring insecurity in the region.
The situation worsened further with the intervention of a militiaman from the NDC-Renovated armed group, who carried out armed robberies on Kalonge/Mubea Hill. Vehicles, particularly motorcycle taxis, were looted, temporarily paralyzing traffic and intensifying the sense of insecurity among road users.
In response to this resurgence of violence, Mwami Kitwana Ngulu Séraphin called on military and administrative authorities to take urgent measures to restore order and protect the civilian population.
Meanwhile, the residents of Kibua continue to live in constant fear, urging the State to strengthen discipline within the regular forces and the wazalendo operating in this volatile part of North Kivu.

title_en: AFC/M23 Rebels Capture "Point Zero," Opening Way to Fizi-Centre
excerpt_en: Mitumba, DRC, January 17, 2026 - The village of "Point Zero", located on the border between the territories of Fizi and Mwenga, on the Mitumba massif, fell to Twirwaneho fighters, allies of the AFC/M23 rebels, on Friday morning, January 16, 2026, after two days of fierce fighting
body_en:
Mitumba, DRC, January 17, 2026 - The village of "Point Zero", located on the border between the territories of Fizi and Mwenga, on the Mitumba massif, fell to Twirwaneho fighters, allies of the AFC/M23 rebels, on Friday morning, January 16, 2026, after two days of fierce fighting against the FARDC, supported by the Wazalendo.
Since Thursday, January 15, heavy fighting had been reported in Tuwetuwe, about 15 km from the Mikenge displaced persons camp in the Itombwe sector, where Twirwaneho fighters pushed the army back towards Point Zero.
According to local sources, the FARDC position was attacked on Friday morning, forcing soldiers to retreat to Mulima in the Basiloca group (Tanganyika sector, Fizi territory).
“We were attacked at 5:00 a.m., and by 9:00 a.m., all FARDC soldiers had left the front and were heading towards Mulima. We found ourselves alone on the battlefield. That is why we were forced to retreat when the enemy occupied the village around 10:00 a.m.,” a security source reported.
Point Zero, built in 2018 by displaced people fleeing intercommunal conflicts in Fizi, Mwenga, and Uvira, was a FARDC stronghold. Its occupation by rebels forced residents to flee in torrential rains to Bilende, Kanguli, Nakiele, Mulima, and Lusuku, where their living conditions remain extremely precarious, with no assistance after abandoning their homes.
The fall of Point Zero, the army’s last stronghold in the area, opens the path for the rebels along the Mulima-Mukera axis towards Fizi-centre, enabling further advances toward Tanganyika province via Misisi, bypassing Baraka.
This development marks a significant strategic gain for the AFC/M23 and allied forces, intensifying the humanitarian and security crisis in the region.

title: South Kivu Government Condemns Looting and Violations by AFC/M23
excerpt: Uvira, South Kivu, DRC, January 17, 2026 - The South Kivu provincial government has denounced the systematic looting, destruction of property, and serious violations of international humanitarian law committed by the Rwandan-backed AFC/M23 rebellion in Uvira. In a statement relea
title_en: South Kivu Government Condemns Looting and Violations by AFC/M23
excerpt_en: Uvira, South Kivu, DRC, January 17, 2026 - The South Kivu provincial government has denounced the systematic looting, destruction of property, and serious violations of international humanitarian law committed by the Rwandan-backed AFC/M23 rebellion in Uvira. In a statement relea
body_en:
Uvira, South Kivu, DRC, January 17, 2026 - The South Kivu provincial government has denounced the systematic looting, destruction of property, and serious violations of international humanitarian law committed by the Rwandan-backed AFC/M23 rebellion in Uvira. In a statement released Friday, January 16, 2026, Governor Jean-Jacques Purusi Sadiki described these acts as extremely serious and indicative of the rebels’ bad faith.
Contrary to the AFC/M23’s correspondence to the UN on January 15, 2026, the government asserts that the rebels organized coordinated operations of looting in Uvira and surrounding areas, demonstrating a flagrant disregard for international humanitarian law and human rights.
“The South Kivu provincial government condemns these criminal acts in the strongest possible terms; it calls upon the international community, the United Nations, the African Union, the ICC, and human rights organizations to document these events and initiate immediate legal proceedings against the perpetrators,” stated the provincial government.
The government emphasized that these acts violate:
Article 33 of the Fourth Geneva Convention (prohibition of pillage)
Article 52 of Additional Protocol I (protection of civilian property)
Article 8 of the Rome Statute of the ICC (pillaging as a war crime)
Various international instruments on property rights and the International Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights
The provincial government warned that these crimes deliberately exacerbate the severe food crisis, raise the cost of living, and deprive the population-mainly dependent on agriculture and livestock-of access to their land and herds, amounting to collective punishment, strictly prohibited under international law.
The statement further revealed that 49 Wowo trucks and 113 Ben trucks were transported from Bukavu under the pretext of moving withdrawn soldiers to the Ruzizi Plain, but were instead used to illegally transport state and private goods to Rwanda. On the night of January 15, 34 Wowo trucks loaded with tar and trucks carrying tricycles essential for livelihoods were seized and moved across the border. Remaining goods were evacuated via Kamanyola, and livestock from the highlands and midlands was driven to Bwegera, depriving locals of essential resources.
Despite the announcement of withdrawal, the AFC/M23 remained in Uvira on January 16, reinforcing positions at Kigongo, 5 km from the city towards Makobola, confirming continued military presence and control.
In a letter to UN Secretary-General António Guterres on January 15, 2026, the AFC/M23 political coordinator, Corneille Nangaa, claimed that Uvira is now under the responsibility of the international community, following their withdrawal announced on December 15, 2025, and dismantled their "observation and surveillance unit", declining future responsibility for the city’s security.
This situation underscores ongoing instability in South Kivu, the continuing humanitarian crisis, and the urgent need for international attention.

title: Burundi Urges US to Strengthen Pressure on Parties Amid Escalating Violence in Eastern DRC
excerpt: Bujumbura, Burundi, January 17, 2026 - Faced with the continued escalation of violence in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), Burundi has called on the United States to increase pressure on the conflicting parties to ensure compliance with their commitments under the Wash
title_en: Burundi Urges US to Strengthen Pressure on Parties Amid Escalating Violence in Eastern DRC
excerpt_en: Bujumbura, Burundi, January 17, 2026 - Faced with the continued escalation of violence in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), Burundi has called on the United States to increase pressure on the conflicting parties to ensure compliance with their commitments under the Wash
body_en:
Bujumbura, Burundi, January 17, 2026 - Faced with the continued escalation of violence in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), Burundi has called on the United States to increase pressure on the conflicting parties to ensure compliance with their commitments under the Washington Accords.
President Évariste Ndayishimiye described the security situation in the Great Lakes region as grim, highlighting violent clashes between government forces and the Rwandan-backed AFC/M23 rebellion, which have caused significant human and material losses and continued territorial gains for the rebels.
During a New Year’s greetings ceremony with the diplomatic and consular corps in Bujumbura on January 14, 2026, Ndayishimiye deplored the ongoing deterioration of the situation despite international diplomatic initiatives led by the African Union (AU). He noted that Burundi has paid a heavy price for the conflict, citing:
Occupation of Congolese territories in the east
Destruction of infrastructure
Massacres of civilians
Annihilation of economic activities
Massive influx of refugees into Burundi
“Despite peace initiatives, UN Security Council resolutions, the Washington and Doha agreements, and efforts by the AU, EAC, and SADC, the situation in eastern DRC remains extremely worrying,” he stated.
President Ndayishimiye, who is also the African Union president-elect, urged the United States, as guarantor of the Washington Accords, to ensure that all parties respect their commitments, stressing the lack of trust between Kinshasa and Kigali.
“When we were in Washington for the signing of the Accords, hope was palpable. Unfortunately, that hope lasted only a few moments. The guarantor must now act,” he declared.
This appeal comes amid a stalled diplomatic process:
Ratified agreements by DRC President Félix Tshisekedi and Rwandan President Paul Kagame are struggling to produce results.
Doha talks, led by the Emir of Qatar, between Kinshasa and the Rwandan-backed AFC/M23, are also failing to achieve concrete outcomes, despite their aim to address the root causes of the conflict, including restoration of state authority and reintegration of armed groups.
Several measures, including the joint communiqué, ceasefire mechanism, declaration of principles, and framework agreement, remain unimplemented, fueling ongoing clashes.
In addition, the national dialogue, called for by socio-political actors to support these peace initiatives, has not yet taken place.
After withdrawing from mediation in March 2025, Angola is now gradually returning to the process, holding consultations with stakeholders. Meanwhile, Togo plans to host a high-level meeting on January 17, 2026, aimed at strengthening the coherence and consolidation of the peace process in the DRC and the Great Lakes region.
This statement by Burundi underscores the urgent need for international action to enforce compliance with agreements and prevent further escalation of violence in eastern DRC.

title: Ndayishimiye Blames Rwanda’s Expansionist Policies for Persistent Tensions in South Kivu
excerpt: Bujumbura, Burundi, January 17, 2026 - President Évariste Ndayishimiye of Burundi spoke out on the ongoing tensions between the Banyamulenge, Bafuliro, and Babembe communities in South Kivu, DRC, asserting that, “Without Rwanda’s expansionist policies, we could have already recon
title_en: Ndayishimiye Blames Rwanda’s Expansionist Policies for Persistent Tensions in South Kivu
excerpt_en: Bujumbura, Burundi, January 17, 2026 - President Évariste Ndayishimiye of Burundi spoke out on the ongoing tensions between the Banyamulenge, Bafuliro, and Babembe communities in South Kivu, DRC, asserting that, “Without Rwanda’s expansionist policies, we could have already recon
body_en:
Bujumbura, Burundi, January 17, 2026 - President Évariste Ndayishimiye of Burundi spoke out on the ongoing tensions between the Banyamulenge, Bafuliro, and Babembe communities in South Kivu, DRC, asserting that, “Without Rwanda’s expansionist policies, we could have already reconciled everyone.”
During the New Year’s greetings ceremony with the diplomatic and consular corps on January 14, 2026, Ndayishimiye reviewed Burundi’s regional responsibilities in 2025, emphasizing the country’s role in protecting civilian populations and promoting peaceful coexistence among local communities in eastern DRC.
“Our officers have experience in reconciliation, not only to ensure the security of the population but also to work towards reconciliation. You witnessed, upon the arrival of Burundian troops, that the Banyamulenge, Babembe, and Bafuliro, who had been fighting each other, immediately reconciled-without Rwanda’s expansionist policy,” he stated.
The Burundian head of state criticized Rwanda’s support of the AFC/M23 rebellion, which led to the occupation of the strategic city of Uvira, before the rebels announced a withdrawal under pressure from the United States-a move contested by the Kinshasa government.
Ndayishimiye praised the cooperation of Kinshasa regarding Congolese refugees hosted in Burundi, noting:
“Even the refugees we are hosting are considered internally displaced persons; they did not flee the government in power, but the aggression of the enemy. We are striving to show them solidarity and are grateful for the Congolese government’s efforts to assist them.”
He highlighted Burundi’s broader regional contributions:
Chairing the Framework Agreement for Peace, Security and Cooperation in the DRC until May 2025.
Chairing COMESA until October 2025.
Holding the first vice-presidency of the African Union since February 2025.
Holding the vice-presidency of the International Conference on the Great Lakes Region.
“These responsibilities have allowed Burundi to actively contribute to conflict resolution in Africa and acquire concrete experience in promoting peace,” Ndayishimiye said.
Addressing the regional dynamics, Ndayishimiye noted that Rwanda continues to provide military support to the AFC/M23 rebels, while Burundi, allied with Kinshasa, is actively fighting alongside the FARDC.
Last December, Burundi accused Rwanda of carrying out “destabilizing activities” along the Congolese border, declaring that its troops deployed in DRC would not withdraw until their mission is fully accomplished.
In a related statement, Burundian Foreign Minister Édouard Bizimana condemned the continuation of hostilities:
“Despite the recently signed ceasefire and peacebuilding agreements, Rwanda continues to deploy its soldiers and carry out attacks against the Burundian National Defence Forces present in the DRC.”
This underscores Burundi’s firm stance in supporting the DRC government and its determination to counter external interference destabilizing the Great Lakes region.

During the New Year’s greetings ceremony with the diplomatic and consular corps on January 14, 2026, Ndayishimiye reviewed Burundi’s regional responsibilities in 2025, emphasizing the country’s role in protecting civilian populations and promoting peaceful coexistence among local communities in eastern DRC.
“Our officers have experience in reconciliation, not only to ensure the security of the population but also to work towards reconciliation. You witnessed, upon the arrival of Burundian troops, that the Banyamulenge, Babembe, and Bafuliro, who had been fighting each other, immediately reconciled-without Rwanda’s expansionist policy,” he stated.
The Burundian head of state criticized Rwanda’s support of the AFC/M23 rebellion, which led to the occupation of the strategic city of Uvira, before the rebels announced a withdrawal under pressure from the United States-a move contested by the Kinshasa government.
Ndayishimiye praised the cooperation of Kinshasa regarding Congolese refugees hosted in Burundi, noting:
“Even the refugees we are hosting are considered internally displaced persons; they did not flee the government in power, but the aggression of the enemy. We are striving to show them solidarity and are grateful for the Congolese government’s efforts to assist them.”
He highlighted Burundi’s broader regional contributions:
Chairing the Framework Agreement for Peace, Security and Cooperation in the DRC until May 2025.
Chairing COMESA until October 2025.
Holding the first vice-presidency of the African Union since February 2025.
Holding the vice-presidency of the International Conference on the Great Lakes Region.
“These responsibilities have allowed Burundi to actively contribute to conflict resolution in Africa and acquire concrete experience in promoting peace,” Ndayishimiye said.
Addressing the regional dynamics, Ndayishimiye noted that Rwanda continues to provide military support to the AFC/M23 rebels, while Burundi, allied with Kinshasa, is actively fighting alongside the FARDC.
Last December, Burundi accused Rwanda of carrying out “destabilizing activities” along the Congolese border, declaring that its troops deployed in DRC would not withdraw until their mission is fully accomplished.
In a related statement, Burundian Foreign Minister Édouard Bizimana condemned the continuation of hostilities:
“Despite the recently signed ceasefire and peacebuilding agreements, Rwanda continues to deploy its soldiers and carry out attacks against the Burundian National Defence Forces present in the DRC.”
This underscores Burundi’s firm stance in supporting the DRC government and its determination to counter external interference destabilizing the Great Lakes region.

title: AFC/M23 Completes Withdrawal from Uvira, Places City Under International Responsibility
excerpt: Uvira, DRC, January 17, 2026 - The AFC/M23 armed group announced on Saturday, January 17, 2026, that it has completed its withdrawal from the city of Uvira in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo, where elements of its military and administrative presence had remained. The moveme
title_en: AFC/M23 Completes Withdrawal from Uvira, Places City Under International Responsibility
excerpt_en: Uvira, DRC, January 17, 2026 - The AFC/M23 armed group announced on Saturday, January 17, 2026, that it has completed its withdrawal from the city of Uvira in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo, where elements of its military and administrative presence had remained. The moveme
body_en:
Uvira, DRC, January 17, 2026 - The AFC/M23 armed group announced on Saturday, January 17, 2026, that it has completed its withdrawal from the city of Uvira in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo, where elements of its military and administrative presence had remained.
The movement had previously announced the withdrawal on January 15, following its seizure of the city in early December, the second largest city in South Kivu province. While most fighters and equipment had already left, reports indicated a residual presence in the city.
On Saturday, a column of fighters in military fatigues, with weapons slung over their shoulders and helmets on, exited the city. Some were on foot, while others traveled aboard trucks. Weapons, including rocket launchers, were visible. Observers counted at least 200 fighters, believed to be the group’s “observation and surveillance unit.”
The AFC/M23 officially declared that it now places Uvira under the full responsibility of the international community, declining all responsibility for the security of the city and its approximately 500,000 residents.
Despite the withdrawal, gunfire, including rocket fire, was reported in the vicinity of Uvira on Saturday morning, leaving local residents with heightened anxiety as the day ended.
This development occurs amid ongoing efforts by the international community, including the African Union, the United States, and regional partners, to stabilize eastern DRC and ensure the protection of civilians following months of armed conflict and territorial disputes.

title: “Human Tragedy” and “Desolation” of Congolese Refugees in Burundi and Tanzania: Government Issues Urgent Appeal for National Solidarity - January 18, 2026
excerpt: Burundi and Tanzania, neighboring countries of the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), are hosting hundreds of thousands of Congolese refugees fleeing clashes between government forces and the Rwandan-backed AFC/M23 rebellion. These hostilities have led to the fall of Uvira and o
title_en: “Human Tragedy” and “Desolation” of Congolese Refugees in Burundi and Tanzania: Government Issues Urgent Appeal for National Solidarity - January 18, 2026
excerpt_en: Burundi and Tanzania, neighboring countries of the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), are hosting hundreds of thousands of Congolese refugees fleeing clashes between government forces and the Rwandan-backed AFC/M23 rebellion. These hostilities have led to the fall of Uvira and o
body_en:
Burundi and Tanzania, neighboring countries of the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), are hosting hundreds of thousands of Congolese refugees fleeing clashes between government forces and the Rwandan-backed AFC/M23 rebellion. These hostilities have led to the fall of Uvira and other localities, expanding rebel influence across North Kivu and South Kivu in eastern DRC.
In response, the Congolese government, led by the Minister of State for Social Affairs and Humanitarian Action, Ève Bazaiba Masudi, conducted a humanitarian mission to both countries to support refugees, deliver assistance, strengthen coordination with host governments, and assess needs alongside international partners.
Following the mission, the minister described the situation as one of “human tragedy” and “desolation.” Speaking at a press conference in Kinshasa on Saturday, January 17, she declared:
“This is a devastating human tragedy. Our compatriots did not flee because of poverty or climate change, but because of the hostilities and the aggression carried out through AFC/M23 proxies.”
Alarming Figures
Burundi currently hosts approximately 250,000 Congolese refugees, spread across seven sites.
The largest site, Busuma, shelters 67,000 people, including 30,000 children and 2,200 unaccompanied minors.
Tanzania is hosting around 87,000 Congolese refugees, including 50,000 children under 18.
Recent arrivals include nearly 10,000 people, and 28 births were recorded on the day of the Congolese delegation’s visit.
Humanitarian Crisis and Funding Shortfalls
The minister warned of a severe shortage of international humanitarian funding, noting that many major donors have reduced or withdrawn support, forcing host countries to shoulder an increasing burden.
Despite its own challenges, the DRC government has become the main donor supporting its refugees, an exceptional step under international humanitarian law.
“Under normal circumstances, the country of origin does not intervene directly. But exceptional circumstances require exceptional measures,” Ève Bazaiba emphasized.
Humanitarian aid delivered included food and non-food items, supported by a special memorandum of understanding between the Congolese government, UNHCR, and Burundi, allowing direct intervention.
Appeal for National Solidarity
Commending the resilience and patriotism of the refugees, who expressed a strong desire to return home once peace is restored, Ève Bazaiba issued a national call to action:
“I appeal to the national solidarity of all Congolese, at home and abroad, to come to the aid of our compatriots in distress. Let us be true soldiers of the digital army and of the nation.”
She urged citizens to mobilize, especially through digital platforms, to defend the national cause and support vulnerable populations.
Security Context
This humanitarian emergency unfolds amid continued territorial gains by the AFC/M23, despite its controversial announcement of withdrawal from Uvira. Congolese authorities believe this declaration is aimed at reducing international pressure, particularly on Kigali, while the rebels continue to consolidate control and establish parallel administrations.
Once a strategic security hub in South Kivu, the fall of Uvira has significantly strengthened the rebellion’s grip on eastern DRC and is viewed as a potential gateway toward the Greater Katanga region, the economic heart of the country.
The Congolese government insists that only sustained international pressure, national solidarity, and concrete humanitarian action can prevent further suffering and restore dignity to displaced populations.

title: Looting and Chaos Force Several Parishes to Cancel Masses
excerpt: Uvira, South Kivu, DRC January 18, 2026 - Looting was reported Sunday in several neighborhoods of Uvira, in South Kivu province, where young people broke into buildings and stole various items, according to witnesses. The morning was marked by repeated gunfire, creating a climate
title_en: Looting and Chaos Force Several Parishes to Cancel Masses
excerpt_en: Uvira, South Kivu, DRC January 18, 2026 - Looting was reported Sunday in several neighborhoods of Uvira, in South Kivu province, where young people broke into buildings and stole various items, according to witnesses. The morning was marked by repeated gunfire, creating a climate
body_en:
Uvira, South Kivu, DRC January 18, 2026 - Looting was reported Sunday in several neighborhoods of Uvira, in South Kivu province, where young people broke into buildings and stole various items, according to witnesses.
The morning was marked by repeated gunfire, creating a climate of insecurity and triggering looting across different parts of the city. Administrative buildings were among the targets.
Due to this deteriorating security situation, several Catholic parishes, including the Uvira Cathedral, were forced to cancel Sunday masses.
At this stage, it remains unclear who controls the situation on the ground. Youths claiming affiliation with the Wazalendo group were seen in some neighborhoods, while the Armed Forces of the Democratic Republic of Congo (FARDC) were reportedly absent from the city.
These events occurred the day after a column of AFC/M23 fighters left Uvira on Saturday, January 17. Armed men in fatigues and helmets were seen departing the city, some on foot and others in trucks, with their number estimated at at least 200.
The AFC/M23 claims this group was its “observation and surveillance unit” and states that their departure marks the completion of its withdrawal from Uvira, announced on January 15, while declaring that it now disclaims all responsibility for the security of the city and its inhabitants.
Gunfire had already been heard around Uvira on Saturday, and anxiety remained high among residents by the end of the day.

body_en:
Kasopo, Walikale, DRC January 19, 2026 - The AFC/M23 rebel position located on Mount Kasopo, on the border between the Kisimba and Ikobo groups in Walikale territory (North Kivu), was targeted early Monday morning, January 19, by FARDC airstrikes.
According to local accounts, a Congolese army drone flew over the area throughout the night from Sunday to Monday. Around 4:00 a.m., residents of surrounding villages were awakened by bomb explosions dropped by the drone on the position.
Last December, this area was the scene of fierce clashes between AFC/M23 rebels and the Wazalendo of the Coalition of Movements for Change (CMC).
Since the beginning of 2026, this is the first rebel position targeted by FARDC airstrikes in the Walikale territory.

title: Over 3,380 Cases of Gender-Based Violence Recorded in December
excerpt: Nyiragongo, Goma and Karisimbi, North Kivu January 19, 2026 - In December alone, more than 3,380 cases of gender-based violence were recorded in the health zones of Nyiragongo, Goma, and Karisimbi, worsening the critical shortage of post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) kits. A humanit
title_en: Over 3,380 Cases of Gender-Based Violence Recorded in December
excerpt_en: Nyiragongo, Goma and Karisimbi, North Kivu January 19, 2026 - In December alone, more than 3,380 cases of gender-based violence were recorded in the health zones of Nyiragongo, Goma, and Karisimbi, worsening the critical shortage of post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) kits. A humanit
body_en:
Nyiragongo, Goma and Karisimbi, North Kivu January 19, 2026 - In December alone, more than 3,380 cases of gender-based violence were recorded in the health zones of Nyiragongo, Goma, and Karisimbi, worsening the critical shortage of post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) kits.
A humanitarian report on North Kivu, particularly in the Nyiragongo territory and the city of Goma, indicates that the security situation remained generally calm, despite brief clashes reported between December 9 and 14 in the villages of Ngangi and Kiziba.
The report highlights that women and girls remain particularly vulnerable to sexual violence, especially when traveling to Virunga National Park to collect food and firewood.
In December, humanitarian partners documented more than 3,380 cases of gender-based violence, a situation aggravated by a critical shortage of PEP kits, the main gap in care for survivors of sexual violence in North Kivu.
For the period from December 2025 to February 2026, the unmet need amounts to 20,484 kits. While support enabled the resupply of 23 out of 34 health zones, 11 zones remain completely without kits.
Since the beginning of 2025, the escalation of the conflict and intensified attacks by the Rwandan-backed AFC/M23 in North and South Kivu have displaced hundreds of thousands of people, worsening an already critical humanitarian crisis. The violence has left hundreds dead and thousands wounded, while blocked roads and insecurity continue to hinder humanitarian access.
Despite these conditions, humanitarian actors continue providing emergency medical care, food assistance, and other life-saving aid, while negotiating access to affected areas. Many voices are now calling on all stakeholders to respect their commitments and take concrete steps to silence the guns and restore peace after nearly three decades of conflict.

excerpt: Burutsi, Walikale January 19, 2026 - The village chief of Burutsi, Mungo Barutsi, was brutally assassinated by unidentified armed men on Sunday, January 18, 2026, in his village located in the Luberike region, in Walikale territory, an area currently controlled by the AFC/M23 reb

body_en:
Burutsi, Walikale January 19, 2026 - The village chief of Burutsi, Mungo Barutsi, was brutally assassinated by unidentified armed men on Sunday, January 18, 2026, in his village located in the Luberike region, in Walikale territory, an area currently controlled by the AFC/M23 rebels since April 2025.
The circumstances of the killing remain unclear, but the assailants fled immediately after the attack.
“An investigation is underway to identify the perpetrators and establish responsibility,” local authorities stated, while calling on the population to remain calm and vigilant.
This assassination further worsens an already fragile security situation in this part of Walikale, marked by the presence of AFC/M23 rebels. Since their takeover, residents have lived in a climate of fear, with reports of abuses, movement restrictions, and attacks on traditional authorities.
Residents are denouncing a resurgence of targeted violence against community leaders, viewed as symbols of social cohesion and local resistance.
The killing comes just one week after a deadly landslide in Burutsi that claimed 28 lives, plunging the community into a severe humanitarian crisis.
“We hadn’t even finished mourning our dead from the landslide, and now we’ve lost our village chief. It’s too much for one community,” said a resident.
The death of Mungo Barutsi has sparked strong emotions, with calls for urgent civilian protection, security for customary authorities, and independent investigations to ensure that justice is served.

title: FARDC Regains Control of Uvira, Denounces Looting Before AFC/M23 Withdrawal
excerpt: Uvira, DRC January 19, 2026 - The Armed Forces of the Democratic Republic of Congo (FARDC) announced that they have regained control of the city of Uvira, in South Kivu, following the withdrawal of the Rwandan army and its AFC/M23 allies. According to the army, the city was retak
title_en: FARDC Regains Control of Uvira, Denounces Looting Before AFC/M23 Withdrawal
excerpt_en: Uvira, DRC January 19, 2026 - The Armed Forces of the Democratic Republic of Congo (FARDC) announced that they have regained control of the city of Uvira, in South Kivu, following the withdrawal of the Rwandan army and its AFC/M23 allies. According to the army, the city was retak
body_en:
Uvira, DRC January 19, 2026 - The Armed Forces of the Democratic Republic of Congo (FARDC) announced that they have regained control of the city of Uvira, in South Kivu, following the withdrawal of the Rwandan army and its AFC/M23 allies. According to the army, the city was retaken on Sunday, January 18, 2026.
In a statement, the FARDC condemned the systematic looting carried out in the city by AFC/M23-RDF forces prior to their evacuation. The army said that around twenty civilians involved in the looting were arrested and will be brought to justice.
“The FARDC are continuing their deployment in and around Uvira to consolidate positions and ensure the safety of people and property,” the statement said.
This development follows a letter sent on January 15, 2026, by the political coordinator of the AFC/M23, Corneille Nangaa, to the United Nations Secretary-General, announcing that the group was placing Uvira under the responsibility of the international community. The movement said this was part of its withdrawal decision, initially announced on December 15, 2025, and reaffirmed as part of its ceasefire commitment.
The rebellion also announced the immediate withdrawal of its “observation and surveillance unit,” declining any further responsibility for the security of Uvira.
However, Congolese authorities have expressed skepticism over this withdrawal, viewing it as an attempt to divert attention and reduce international pressure, particularly on Kigali, which Kinshasa considers the main supporter of the rebellion. On the ground, the AFC/M23 continues territorial advances and is establishing a parallel administration outside government control.
Uvira, a strategic city in South Kivu, had fallen under rebel control, strengthening the group’s hold over North and South Kivu. The city is considered a key security hub, whose control could facilitate further advances toward the Greater Katanga region, the economic heartland of the Democratic Republic of Congo.

title: FARDC Post Set on Fire by Wazalendo Militiamen
excerpt: Misevere, Lubero January 20, 2026 - A post belonging to the Armed Forces of the Democratic Republic of Congo (FARDC) was set on fire overnight from Monday to Tuesday in Misevere, a village near Musienene, close to the Musienene primary school, in the Baswagha chiefdom of Lubero t
title_en: FARDC Post Set on Fire by Wazalendo Militiamen
excerpt_en: Misevere, Lubero January 20, 2026 - A post belonging to the Armed Forces of the Democratic Republic of Congo (FARDC) was set on fire overnight from Monday to Tuesday in Misevere, a village near Musienene, close to the Musienene primary school, in the Baswagha chiefdom of Lubero t
body_en:
Misevere, Lubero January 20, 2026 - A post belonging to the Armed Forces of the Democratic Republic of Congo (FARDC) was set on fire overnight from Monday to Tuesday in Misevere, a village near Musienene, close to the Musienene primary school, in the Baswagha chiefdom of Lubero territory, North Kivu.
The fire is attributed to Wazalendo militiamen. The incident reportedly occurred while the FARDC soldiers who normally occupy the post were absent, having reportedly left on a mission to Beni territory, leaving the position undefended. A local civil society leader described the act as a serious offense.
The military administrator of Lubero territory confirmed the incident but did not provide details on the circumstances or measures taken.
This attack comes just days after a similar incident in the same region. On January 8, 2026, an abandoned FARDC position was set on fire in Vusigha, in the Musienene-Katholo area, Ngulo group, also within the Baswagha chiefdom. The soldiers had left the site on January 6, 2026, to return to Beni, after which all barracks built by loyalist forces were burned to the ground by unidentified individuals.

title: Eight Suspects Presented to Authorities After Deadly Customary Conflict

title_en: Eight Suspects Presented to Authorities After Deadly Customary Conflict
excerpt_en: Bagata, Kwilu January 20, 2026 -- Eight suspects accused of murder and arson that destroyed 34 houses in the village of Lunkuni, located in the Manzasay sector of Bagata territory, were presented to the Governor of Kwilu by the police on Tuesday. They were arrested in connection
body_en:
Bagata, Kwilu January 20, 2026 -- Eight suspects accused of murder and arson that destroyed 34 houses in the village of Lunkuni, located in the Manzasay sector of Bagata territory, were presented to the Governor of Kwilu by the police on Tuesday.
They were arrested in connection with a customary conflict that led to the assassination of the chief of the Bamenga Lokwa group on January 5 in Lunkuni.
In addition to the local chief, three other deaths were reported on January 7, including two people who were beheaded.
Police also handed over several 12-gauge shotguns recovered from the suspects.
Two weeks after the violence, a large portion of the population remains displaced, hiding in the forest. Authorities confirmed the deployment of the Northern Mobile Intervention Group to stabilize the area and facilitate the return of residents to their homes.
“This was a poorly managed customary conflict that resulted in the assassination of Chief Bamenga. In retaliation, the deceased’s brothers burned down 34 houses. Police were immediately deployed to restore public order. Many residents have not yet returned home and remain in the bush. A special intervention unit is being sent to enable their safe return,” stated Chief Commissioner Camille Atungale, police spokesperson.
Authorities also indicated that additional bodies may not yet have been recovered due to ongoing tensions between rival families competing for customary authority.

title: AFC/M23 Rebels Launch Attacks on FARDC in Mpombi and Iteya
excerpt: Pinga, Walikale January 21, 2026 - Violent clashes erupted on Wednesday morning, January 21, between AFC/M23 rebels and the Armed Forces of the Democratic Republic of Congo (FARDC), supported by the Wazalendo, in the localities of Mpombi and Iteya, part of the Kisimba group in Wa
title_en: AFC/M23 Rebels Launch Attacks on FARDC in Mpombi and Iteya
excerpt_en: Pinga, Walikale January 21, 2026 - Violent clashes erupted on Wednesday morning, January 21, between AFC/M23 rebels and the Armed Forces of the Democratic Republic of Congo (FARDC), supported by the Wazalendo, in the localities of Mpombi and Iteya, part of the Kisimba group in Wa
body_en:
Pinga, Walikale January 21, 2026 - Violent clashes erupted on Wednesday morning, January 21, between AFC/M23 rebels and the Armed Forces of the Democratic Republic of Congo (FARDC), supported by the Wazalendo, in the localities of Mpombi and Iteya, part of the Kisimba group in Walikale territory, North Kivu.
The rebels launched simultaneous attacks against army positions starting around 10:00 a.m., with heavy and light weapons fire reported, plunging the local population into widespread fear.
The administrative secretary of the Kisimba group, Lavie Changwi, confirmed the clashes and said that civilians were forced to flee their homes, seeking refuge in the surrounding forests.
“Mpombi and Iteya are key strongholds for the protection of Pinga. The situation is very worrying due to the intensity of the fighting,” he stated.
These towns, held by FARDC and Wazalendo forces, occupy a mountainous area overlooking Pinga and are considered crucial for the town’s defense.
This attack comes amid an already fragile security context. In December 2025, authorities were alerted to the strengthening of rebel positions in Mpety, considered the main AFC/M23 stronghold in the Pinga region. Reports indicated that rebels were preparing offensives targeting Pinga.
In early January 2026, the rebels attempted to seize Mpombi and Iteya but were repelled by FARDC forces, retreating to their rear base in Mpety.
Following Wednesday's assaults, no official casualty figures have been released. The situation remains tense and unpredictable in the combat zones around Pinga.

title: Five Civilians Killed and Homes Burned in New ADF Attack
excerpt: Mavwe-Mavwe, Lubero, January 22, 2026 - Five civilians were killed and about ten houses burned during an attack by Allied Democratic Forces (ADF) fighters on the night of Tuesday, January 21, in the Mwenye region of Lubero territory, North Kivu. The incident occurred in the villa
title_en: Five Civilians Killed and Homes Burned in New ADF Attack
excerpt_en: Mavwe-Mavwe, Lubero, January 22, 2026 - Five civilians were killed and about ten houses burned during an attack by Allied Democratic Forces (ADF) fighters on the night of Tuesday, January 21, in the Mwenye region of Lubero territory, North Kivu. The incident occurred in the villa
body_en:
Mavwe-Mavwe, Lubero, January 22, 2026 - Five civilians were killed and about ten houses burned during an attack by Allied Democratic Forces (ADF) fighters on the night of Tuesday, January 21, in the Mwenye region of Lubero territory, North Kivu. The incident occurred in the village of Mavwe-Mavwe, in the Mandelya locality, with four women among the victims.
Local authorities reported that the attackers moved freely across the territory, particularly in the Bapere sector and certain areas of the Baswagha chiefdom. In addition to the burned houses and fatalities, other civilians are missing.
This assault follows a previous ADF attack on Tuesday, January 13, in which five civilians were killed, two abducted, and several houses set on fire in a village about 17 kilometers west of Masoya, the main town of the Mwenye group.
Shortly before that, ADF fighters struck the village of Byambwe, the main town of the Manzia group, located along the Butembo-Manguredjipa road in the Baswagha chiefdom.
Furthermore, the bodies of six civilians killed by ADF rebels on Friday, January 16, were recovered and buried the following Monday in Pokia, a village in Tombolea, Bapakombe group, Bapere sector, also in Lubero territory.
These repeated attacks underscore the ongoing insecurity and vulnerability of civilians in North Kivu, highlighting the urgent need for strengthened protection measures in the region.

Kanyabayonga, Rutshuru January 22, 2026 - A local chief and his wife were killed by unidentified armed men on the evening of Wednesday, January 21, in the Kanyabayonga group of the Bwito chiefdom, Rutshuru territory, North Kivu, an area currently under AFC/M23 control.
The victims, Muhindo Mungumwa Claude and his spouse, were attacked around 11:00 p.m., when assailants stormed their residence and opened fire, local community leaders reported. The bodies were discovered in the early hours of Thursday, January 22. One of their children also remains missing.
Muhindo Mungumwa Claude had been appointed as head of the Kanyabayonga group by the AFC/M23, which controls the region. He was a well-known figure in the Kanyabayonga-Bwito community, previously serving as secretary to the former chief of the Lukira Pandasi community, now based in Beni.
Local leaders condemned the assassination and demanded explanations from the rebel authorities.
This incident echoes a similar attack in October in Buramba, where Chief Maliro was killed by unidentified gunmen who broke into his home around midnight and stabbed him to death, according to local accounts.
The killing of Chief Mungumwa and his wife highlights the persistent insecurity in rebel-held areas of North Kivu and the targeting of community leaders, further destabilizing local governance structures.

title: MSF Responds to Surge in Wounded Amid Escalating Violence
excerpt: Nyanzale, Rutshuru January 23, 2026 - Doctors Without Borders (MSF) has raised the alarm over an influx of wounded in Nyanzale, following intensified clashes between AFC/M23 rebels and Wazalendo militias, part of the Collective of Movements for Change (CMC), in Rutshuru territory
title_en: MSF Responds to Surge in Wounded Amid Escalating Violence
excerpt_en: Nyanzale, Rutshuru January 23, 2026 - Doctors Without Borders (MSF) has raised the alarm over an influx of wounded in Nyanzale, following intensified clashes between AFC/M23 rebels and Wazalendo militias, part of the Collective of Movements for Change (CMC), in Rutshuru territory
body_en:
Nyanzale, Rutshuru January 23, 2026 - Doctors Without Borders (MSF) has raised the alarm over an influx of wounded in Nyanzale, following intensified clashes between AFC/M23 rebels and Wazalendo militias, part of the Collective of Movements for Change (CMC), in Rutshuru territory, North Kivu.
Since January 20, MSF teams have been supporting the Nyanzale health center, providing medical and logistical assistance to 32 people injured by bullets and shrapnel, most of them civilians.
According to patient testimonies, the wounded began arriving on January 19 after an attack by Wazalendo militiamen. Civilians performing community work, locally called “salogo,” were caught in the crossfire. Several homes were reported burned during the violence.
MSF is also carrying out humanitarian support, including the construction of toilets, distribution of drinking water, and health promotion in vulnerable areas. The organization warns that the affected population is living in precarious conditions, with limited access to hygiene, adequate shelter, food, and basic necessities.
The security situation in Nyanzale remains tense. Fighting resumed Sunday afternoon, January 19, after a brief lull, with intense crossfire reported throughout the area. Civilians who had recently returned from displacement barricaded themselves in their homes for safety.
The Wazalendo faction of the CMC denounced a bomb attack on January 18 that struck several localities, including Nyarubande, Burambo, Muhanga, the center of Kihondo, and Kiyeye, and vowed swift retaliation. Further clashes were reported near Katsiru.
The provisional toll from the violence includes two civilians killed in Kihondo-a man and a woman-and ten houses burned in Nyarubande, Bwito chiefdom.
The situation underscores the persistent vulnerability of civilians in North Kivu amid ongoing armed clashes, highlighting the urgent need for humanitarian assistance and protection.

title: Surge in Injuries Strains Hospital Capacity Amid Ongoing Violence
excerpt: Fizi, South Kivu January 23, 2026 - The escalation of armed violence in Fizi territory, South Kivu, since late December 2025, has led to a dramatic rise in gunshot wounds and severely limited access to healthcare. The Fizi General Referral Hospital (HGR), supported by the Interna
title_en: Surge in Injuries Strains Hospital Capacity Amid Ongoing Violence
excerpt_en: Fizi, South Kivu January 23, 2026 - The escalation of armed violence in Fizi territory, South Kivu, since late December 2025, has led to a dramatic rise in gunshot wounds and severely limited access to healthcare. The Fizi General Referral Hospital (HGR), supported by the Interna
body_en:
Fizi, South Kivu January 23, 2026 - The escalation of armed violence in Fizi territory, South Kivu, since late December 2025, has led to a dramatic rise in gunshot wounds and severely limited access to healthcare. The Fizi General Referral Hospital (HGR), supported by the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC), is now facing critical overcrowding.
According to ICRC reports, the number of wounded patients has quadrupled in just a few weeks. As of January 18, 2026, the hospital was treating 115 wounded patients, far exceeding its official capacity of 25 beds.
Medical staff report that many patients arrive too late for timely care, often with infected or complicated injuries, due to delays in treatment at peripheral health centers. “Most of the new patients had infected wounds from lack of adequate care. Many were unable to receive proper stabilization in the local facilities they passed through,” explained one hospital physician.
To respond to the crisis, the ICRC established additional tents to expand treatment capacity and deployed an emergency surgical team on January 10, 2026 to support local staff.
The ICRC highlights that these late arrivals reflect the collapse of frontline healthcare facilities near the conflict zones. Persistent insecurity, looting, shortages of medicines, and the departure of medical personnel have left several health centers paralyzed, leaving civilians and combatants alike without access to timely care.
The situation in Fizi underscores the humanitarian toll of the ongoing conflict in South Kivu and the urgent need for support to restore healthcare services for affected populations.

title: Clashes Erupt Between FARDC and AFC/M23 Rebels in Strategic Pinga Area
excerpt: Buma, Walikale, DRC - Violent clashes erupted on Friday, January 23, between AFC/M23 rebels and the Armed Forces of the Democratic Republic of Congo (FARDC), supported by the Wazalendo militia, in Buma and the Ciprès Mountains, along the border between Baljnda and Banakindi in th
title_en: Clashes Erupt Between FARDC and AFC/M23 Rebels in Strategic Pinga Area
excerpt_en: Buma, Walikale, DRC - Violent clashes erupted on Friday, January 23, between AFC/M23 rebels and the Armed Forces of the Democratic Republic of Congo (FARDC), supported by the Wazalendo militia, in Buma and the Ciprès Mountains, along the border between Baljnda and Banakindi in th
body_en:
Buma, Walikale, DRC - Violent clashes erupted on Friday, January 23, between AFC/M23 rebels and the Armed Forces of the Democratic Republic of Congo (FARDC), supported by the Wazalendo militia, in Buma and the Ciprès Mountains, along the border between Baljnda and Banakindi in the Pinga region of Walikale territory, North Kivu.
Fighting reportedly began around 5:00 a.m., when rebel elements launched attacks on FARDC positions. The clashes occurred along the road linking Balinda and Banakindi, in the Kisimba region, a strategic mountainous area overlooking Munsanga, considered a key security stronghold for Pinga.
Heavy and light weapons fire reverberated for hours, sending residents fleeing into nearby forests in fear for their safety. Many villagers from Munsanga, Buma, and surrounding communities remain displaced as a result of the attacks.
By midday, military authorities had not released official figures on casualties or material damage. However, local sources indicate that the FARDC mounted a resolute defense, attempting to contain the rebels’ advance and protect Pinga, an important administrative and humanitarian center in the region.
These clashes come amid a fragile security situation in Walikale, characterized by repeated armed attacks, population displacement, and a worsening humanitarian crisis. Civil society groups in the region have urged the government and loyalist forces to reinforce security measures to prevent the fall of Pinga, which could have serious consequences for thousands of civilians already living in precarious conditions.

excerpt_en: Buleusa, Walikale, DRC January 23, 2026 - A rebel position of the AFC/M23 was destroyed by airstrikes conducted by the Armed Forces of the Democratic Republic of Congo (FARDC) on Friday, January 23, in Buleusa, located in the Ikobo region of Walikale territory, North Kivu. The op
body_en:
Buleusa, Walikale, DRC January 23, 2026 - A rebel position of the AFC/M23 was destroyed by airstrikes conducted by the Armed Forces of the Democratic Republic of Congo (FARDC) on Friday, January 23, in Buleusa, located in the Ikobo region of Walikale territory, North Kivu.
The operation reportedly took place around 1:00 p.m., when an FARDC drone targeted the rebel camp, a strategic site in the area. Local sources reported that the position was completely destroyed, with flames and thick smoke visible from afar, causing panic among the population.
Witnesses said the rebels fled after the bombing, seeking refuge in nearby parts of the town. “We saw flames and thick smoke rising from the camp. The rebels ran immediately,” one resident said.
Military sources confirmed that the strike is part of ongoing operations in Walikale, where the AFC/M23 has been attempting to consolidate its positions in recent weeks. The FARDC has increasingly deployed drones to locate and neutralize rebel bases, a strategy that appears to be yielding results on the ground.
Despite this success, the security situation remains fragile, with residents of Buleusa and surrounding villages fearing reprisals or renewed clashes. No official figures on rebel casualties have been released, but the strike reportedly inflicted significant material losses and dealt a major blow to the operational capacity of the AFC/M23 in the area.

title: DRC - U.S. Africa Command Explores Security Cooperation with FARDC
excerpt: Kinshasa, January 23, 2026 - U.S. Africa Command (AFRICOM) visited the Armed Forces of the Democratic Republic of Congo (FARDC) on January 22 to explore opportunities for enhanced security cooperation, reflecting a growing strategic rapprochement between Kinshasa and Washington.
title_en: DRC - U.S. Africa Command Explores Security Cooperation with FARDC
excerpt_en: Kinshasa, January 23, 2026 - U.S. Africa Command (AFRICOM) visited the Armed Forces of the Democratic Republic of Congo (FARDC) on January 22 to explore opportunities for enhanced security cooperation, reflecting a growing strategic rapprochement between Kinshasa and Washington.
body_en:
Kinshasa, January 23, 2026 - U.S. Africa Command (AFRICOM) visited the Armed Forces of the Democratic Republic of Congo (FARDC) on January 22 to explore opportunities for enhanced security cooperation, reflecting a growing strategic rapprochement between Kinshasa and Washington.
Colonel Michael Gacheru, head of the AFRICOM delegation, praised the FARDC’s willingness to collaborate, stating, “This visit demonstrates our unwavering support for the FARDC and the DRC government,” and underscoring efforts to promote peace through strengthened military cooperation. The discussions also included Congolese Generals Jules Banza Mwilambwe and Marcel Lukwikila.
The visit coincides with recent peace agreements between the DRC and Rwanda and bilateral economic accords with the United States. As part of this evolving framework, a memorandum of understanding on defense and security was signed to deepen cooperation, particularly in training, equipping forces, and protecting critical infrastructure.
To date, the U.S. Embassy has supported professional training programs for the FARDC, as well as initiatives to train and equip police officers and construct police stations. Officials note that a similar military cooperation protocol was signed in 2020, though its implementation had been limited, signaling that current efforts aim to build on and expand past agreements.

title: Rwanda Confirms Security Coordination with AFC/M23 in Eastern DRC
excerpt: Kinshasa/Washington, January 23, 2026 - For the first time, Rwanda has officially acknowledged coordinating with the AFC/M23 rebel group operating in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC). Kigali frames this collaboration as a defensive measure, aimed at protecting Tutsi pop
title_en: Rwanda Confirms Security Coordination with AFC/M23 in Eastern DRC
excerpt_en: Kinshasa/Washington, January 23, 2026 - For the first time, Rwanda has officially acknowledged coordinating with the AFC/M23 rebel group operating in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC). Kigali frames this collaboration as a defensive measure, aimed at protecting Tutsi pop
body_en:
Kinshasa/Washington, January 23, 2026 - For the first time, Rwanda has officially acknowledged coordinating with the AFC/M23 rebel group operating in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC). Kigali frames this collaboration as a defensive measure, aimed at protecting Tutsi populations in the region and preventing any resurgence of genocidal violence.
In a statement addressed to the U.S. Congress on January 22, Rwandan Ambassador to the United States Mathilde Mukantabana said the partnership also facilitated the unilateral withdrawal of AFC/M23 forces from the city of Uvira, signaling the rebel group’s commitment to de-escalation.
“Following the escalation, the AFC/M23, with the support of my government, recently carried out a unilateral withdrawal from Uvira, demonstrating its commitment to reducing tensions,” the ambassador said.
Mukantabana outlined the framework of the collaboration, emphasizing that while Rwanda and AFC/M23 share a common interest in protecting Tutsi communities from the FDLR and other armed groups, Rwanda’s involvement is strictly defensive, conditional, and temporary. She stressed that Rwanda does not seek to influence the internal politics of the DRC.

title: FARDC Drones Strike AFC/M23 Position in Kikuku
excerpt: Rutshuru, North Kivu, January 23, 2026 - Military pressure on AFC/M23 rebels is intensifying in North Kivu. Following airstrikes in Buleusa, the Armed Forces of the Democratic Republic of Congo (FARDC) targeted another rebel position in Kikuku, located in the Bwito chiefdom, Ruts
title_en: FARDC Drones Strike AFC/M23 Position in Kikuku
excerpt_en: Rutshuru, North Kivu, January 23, 2026 - Military pressure on AFC/M23 rebels is intensifying in North Kivu. Following airstrikes in Buleusa, the Armed Forces of the Democratic Republic of Congo (FARDC) targeted another rebel position in Kikuku, located in the Bwito chiefdom, Ruts
body_en:
Rutshuru, North Kivu, January 23, 2026 - Military pressure on AFC/M23 rebels is intensifying in North Kivu. Following airstrikes in Buleusa, the Armed Forces of the Democratic Republic of Congo (FARDC) targeted another rebel position in Kikuku, located in the Bwito chiefdom, Rutshuru territory.
Shortly after 2 p.m., a FARDC drone carried out a precision strike near the administrative office of the Bwito chiefdom, destroying the rebel position completely, according to local sources. Residents reported loud explosions, thick black smoke, and widespread panic.
No official figures have been released regarding casualties. However, the attack reportedly caused significant material damage, including the total destruction of the rebel camp.
Observers note that the FARDC’s increased use of drones marks a new stage in operations, aimed at weakening rebel capacities and reducing their ability to carry out attacks in the region.
Despite this military pressure, tension remains high in Kikuku, with civilians continuing to bear the brunt of the ongoing insecurity in eastern DRC.
Conclusion
The reporting period from January 12 to 24, 2026, depicts a Democratic Republic of Congo at a critical crossroads, defined by a complex interplay of persistent conflict, intensive diplomacy, and strategic economic shifts. While high-level mediation through the Washington and Doha processes continues, the security situation in the east remains volatile, marked by shifting rebel positions, humanitarian distress for hundreds of thousands of displaced persons, and a growing reliance on drone technology in military operations. Concurrently, the government is asserting greater economic sovereignty, particularly in the mining sector, and pursuing ambitious internal infrastructure projects despite facing significant domestic political opposition and international legal challenges. Ultimately, the path toward lasting stability appears to hinge on the successful operationalization of regional monitoring mechanisms and the realization of a truly inclusive national dialogue
Overviews :
1. Diplomatic & Political Overview: A Region at a Crossroads
The DRC is currently navigating a period of intense but stalled diplomacy. While multiple peace frameworks exist-specifically the Washington and Doha processes-there is a palpable lack of trust between Kinshasa and Kigali.
The "Lomé Momentum": Togo has emerged as a key African mediator, hosting high-level sessions to harmonize these disparate peace initiatives.
Domestic Political Tension: Internally, the government faces a fractured landscape. The exile of figures like Seth Kikuni and the arrest of others like Aubin Minaku signal a deepening rift between the current administration and the opposition.
The Call for Dialogue: International partners, including Belgium’s King Philippe, are increasingly pushing for an "inclusive national dialogue" to address the root causes of instability.
2. Security Overview: Technological Shifts and Precarious Ceasefires
The security landscape in eastern DRC remains volatile, characterized by a "frozen conflict" that frequently thaws into violence.
Drone Warfare: A notable shift in FARDC tactics is the increased use of precision drone strikes to target AFC/M23 positions, as seen in Buleusa and Kikuku.
The Uvira Vacuum: The AFC/M23’s tactical withdrawal from Uvira has created a complex security environment, with the rebels officially placing the city under "international responsibility" while the government views the move as a strategy to deflect international pressure.
Reinforcements vs. Retreats: While rebels withdrew from some areas, they simultaneously reinforced positions in others, such as Masisi, indicating they are preparing for potential counter-offensives.
3. Economic & Technical Overview: Asserting Sovereignty
Kinshasa is actively seeking to reclaim control over its national resources and public systems, though this has led to significant legal and logistical friction.
Resource Nationalism: Gécamines’ decision to directly purchase 100,000 tons of copper from the Tenke Fungurume Mine for the US market is a landmark move to assert state sovereignty over metal pricing and marketing.
Infrastructure Struggles: Efforts to rehabilitate vital infrastructure, such as the Bandundu and Kikwit airports, have been plagued by technical failures and contract terminations, highlighting the challenges of internal development.
Legal Battles: The $4 billion lawsuit by PayServices underscores the risks and complexities the DRC faces as it attempts to modernize and digitize its state payment systems.
4. Humanitarian Overview: A Growing Regional Crisis
The human cost of the conflict has reached a "devastating human tragedy," as described by government officials.
Mass Displacement: Over 200,000 Congolese refugees are now in Burundi alone, with transit centers operating at 200% capacity.
Medical System Collapse: Frontline health facilities in zones like Fizi and Walikale are overwhelmed by gunshot victims and suffering from acute shortages of medicine and nutritional products.
Conservation at Risk: Even conservation efforts are caught in the crossfire; while Virunga National Park recorded a rare mountain gorilla birth, the park remains under threat from the ongoing presence of armed groups.
By Glad MUSEMA
Jeff Buleli
