title: Kinshasa-DRC: Senior Military Officers Transferred to Ndolo Prison Amid Treason Investigations
excerpt: On January 7, 2026, Gen. Franck Ntumba Buamunda, former head of the military office at the presidential palace, and Gen. Maj Christian Ndaywel Okura, former head of the military intelligence service, were transferred to Ndolo military prison in Kinshasa. Gen. Ntumba had been arre
title_en: Kinshasa-DRC: Senior Military Officers Transferred to Ndolo Prison Amid Treason Investigations
excerpt_en: On January 7, 2026, Gen. Franck Ntumba Buamunda, former head of the military office at the presidential palace, and Gen. Maj Christian Ndaywel Okura, former head of the military intelligence service, were transferred to Ndolo military prison in Kinshasa. Gen. Ntumba had been arre
body_en:
On January 7, 2026, Gen. Franck Ntumba Buamunda, former head of the military office at the presidential palace, and Gen. Maj Christian Ndaywel Okura, former head of the military intelligence service, were transferred to Ndolo military prison in Kinshasa.
Gen. Ntumba had been arrested in July 2025, while Ndaywel was detained in August 2025, shortly after leaving the intelligence service. Both were initially held in the National Security Council cell during ongoing investigations. Their transfer to Ndolo marks the continuation of their cases at the High Military Court.
Other senior officers reported to have spent the night at Ndolo include Brig Gen Benjamin Katende Batubadila, Brig Gen Antoine Longondjo Lobandi, Col Jules Boele Bagolome, and Maj Jean-Lambert Embole Ngondili. The detainees face charges including conspiracy against the Head of State, treason, attempted murder, spreading rumors, and disobeying orders.
Meanwhile, Gen. Christian Tshiwewe Songesha, former Chief of Staff of the FARDC and military advisor to President Félix Tshisekedi, remains in the High Security Council cell. He has been accused of plotting to assassinate the president, and the Secretary General of the ruling UDPS party, Augustin Kabuya, stated that Tshiwewe confessed to the alleged plot.
Military expert Jean-Jacques Wondo has raised concerns that several of these detentions may be unjust or politically motivated, aimed at removing senior officers from military decision-making. Officers cited by Wondo include Gen. Freddy Kalume, Gen. Maj Frank Ngama Lebe, and Gen. Dieudonné Mutupeke Kiamata, all accused in connection with alleged plots against President Tshisekedi.

title: Trial of Sheikh Bahame Hassan Continues in Closed Session
excerpt: Nyamata, Bugesera District - 8 January 2026: The Nyamata Primary Court has ordered that the trial of Sheikh Bahame Hassan, Coordinator of the Gitagata Ngororamuco Center, suspected of sexually abusing some beneficiaries of the center, continue behind closed doors. Bahame was arre
title_en: Trial of Sheikh Bahame Hassan Continues in Closed Session
excerpt_en: Nyamata, Bugesera District - 8 January 2026: The Nyamata Primary Court has ordered that the trial of Sheikh Bahame Hassan, Coordinator of the Gitagata Ngororamuco Center, suspected of sexually abusing some beneficiaries of the center, continue behind closed doors. Bahame was arre
body_en:
Nyamata, Bugesera District - 8 January 2026: The Nyamata Primary Court has ordered that the trial of Sheikh Bahame Hassan, Coordinator of the Gitagata Ngororamuco Center, suspected of sexually abusing some beneficiaries of the center, continue behind closed doors.
Bahame was arrested on 16 December 2025 following a multi-day investigation into allegations that he exploited female victims at the center for sexual purposes, under the pretense of helping them or connecting them with families.
The Rwanda Investigation Bureau (RIB) charged him with abusing his legal authority for personal gain and soliciting or performing sexual acts.
The hearing on detention and provisional release, initially scheduled for 6 January 2026, was postponed to 8 January after the Prosecution presented evidence of its participation in the investigation. During the hearing, Bahame’s lawyer, Me Nyembo Emeline, requested that the trial continue in camera due to the sensitive nature of the case. The court granted this request, clearing the courtroom while proceedings continued.
Although the trial is being held privately, the judgment will be read publicly, in accordance with Rwandan criminal law. The court’s decision is expected to be announced on 13 January 2026.
The investigation revealed that Bahame allegedly provided illegal benefits to individuals for personal sexual gratification. Under Article 6 of Rwanda’s Anti-Corruption Law, soliciting, accepting, or promising sexual favors for personal or unlawful gain is a punishable offense, carrying prison terms from 5 to 10 years and fines ranging from 1,000,000 to 10,000,000 Rwf, depending on the nature of the offense.
Sheikh Bahame Hassan was appointed Director of the Gitagata Cultural Center in 2021 and previously gained public recognition while leading the Rubavu District. The RIB continues its investigation into his alleged crimes.

title: Burundi Tightens Airport Controls to Stop Military Desertions Linked to DRC Conflict
excerpt: Bujumbura, December 29, 2025 The Government of Burundi has introduced new measures to block the escape route used by soldiers fleeing abroad, amid growing concern that military desertions could increase due to the country’s involvement in the conflict in eastern Democratic Republ
title_en: Burundi Tightens Airport Controls to Stop Military Desertions Linked to DRC Conflict
excerpt_en: Bujumbura, December 29, 2025 The Government of Burundi has introduced new measures to block the escape route used by soldiers fleeing abroad, amid growing concern that military desertions could increase due to the country’s involvement in the conflict in eastern Democratic Republ
body_en:
Bujumbura, December 29, 2025
The Government of Burundi has introduced new measures to block the escape route used by soldiers fleeing abroad, amid growing concern that military desertions could increase due to the country’s involvement in the conflict in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC).
According to the Burundian presidency, between 2023 and August 2025, at least 14 senior military officers deserted the national army and fled abroad after Burundi’s forces became engaged in fighting against the AFC/M23. Those officers include nine colonels and five majors, alongside numerous soldiers of lower rank.
The most recent confirmed defection is that of Lt. Irambona Désiré, whose desertion was officially recognized through a presidential decree signed on December 22, 2025, by President Évariste Ndayishimiye.
Sources in Bujumbura indicate that deserters come from various ranks, though the majority are lieutenants and captains. Many reportedly travel to European countries, Canada, or Dubai in the United Arab Emirates, where they seek civilian employment.
Several soldiers who have fled say they do not understand why they were deployed to fight in the war in eastern DRC, describing fear of prolonged involvement in a foreign conflict as a major reason for desertion.
Until recently, desertion through legal travel channels was reportedly facilitated by corruption. Officers from the Special Police Service responsible for issuing passports (PAFE) allegedly demanded bribes and instructed soldiers to obtain identity cards under false names, which were then used to secure travel documents.
Following the defeat of AFC/M23 forces in several areas of South Kivu Province, including Katogota, Lubarika, Sange, Kiliba, and the city of Uvira, Burundian authorities grew increasingly concerned that more soldiers would attempt to flee with the assistance of corrupt officials.
On December 29, Pacifique Nininahazwe, head of the human rights organization FOCODE, announced that several soldiers had recently been arrested at Bujumbura International Airport while attempting to travel to Dubai in search of work. Some of the arrests reportedly involved PAFE officers suspected of facilitating illegal departures.
Earlier, on December 22, Burundi’s Minister of Foreign Affairs, Dr. Édouard Bizimana, issued a decree introducing stricter requirements for Burundians seeking employment abroad. While officially applicable to all citizens, multiple sources say the measure primarily targets military personnel attempting to desert.
Under the new rules, any Burundian departing for work abroad must present an identity card issued by the competent ministry, a signed contract from the employer, and authorization from a family member. For soldiers, this effectively requires documentation from the Ministry of Defense and Veterans Affairs, which is not issued to active-duty personnel.
Previously, Burundi’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs only monitored labor migration to countries that had formal worker-exchange agreements with Burundi. The new directive expands oversight to all destination countries, including those without bilateral agreements.
The move signals a significant tightening of controls as Burundi seeks to curb military desertions amid growing domestic unease over its role in the DRC conflict.

The Government of Burundi has introduced new measures to block the escape route used by soldiers fleeing abroad, amid growing concern that military desertions could increase due to the country’s involvement in the conflict in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC).
According to the Burundian presidency, between 2023 and August 2025, at least 14 senior military officers deserted the national army and fled abroad after Burundi’s forces became engaged in fighting against the AFC/M23. Those officers include nine colonels and five majors, alongside numerous soldiers of lower rank.
The most recent confirmed defection is that of Lt. Irambona Désiré, whose desertion was officially recognized through a presidential decree signed on December 22, 2025, by President Évariste Ndayishimiye.
Sources in Bujumbura indicate that deserters come from various ranks, though the majority are lieutenants and captains. Many reportedly travel to European countries, Canada, or Dubai in the United Arab Emirates, where they seek civilian employment.
Several soldiers who have fled say they do not understand why they were deployed to fight in the war in eastern DRC, describing fear of prolonged involvement in a foreign conflict as a major reason for desertion.
Until recently, desertion through legal travel channels was reportedly facilitated by corruption. Officers from the Special Police Service responsible for issuing passports (PAFE) allegedly demanded bribes and instructed soldiers to obtain identity cards under false names, which were then used to secure travel documents.
Following the defeat of AFC/M23 forces in several areas of South Kivu Province, including Katogota, Lubarika, Sange, Kiliba, and the city of Uvira, Burundian authorities grew increasingly concerned that more soldiers would attempt to flee with the assistance of corrupt officials.
On December 29, Pacifique Nininahazwe, head of the human rights organization FOCODE, announced that several soldiers had recently been arrested at Bujumbura International Airport while attempting to travel to Dubai in search of work. Some of the arrests reportedly involved PAFE officers suspected of facilitating illegal departures.
Earlier, on December 22, Burundi’s Minister of Foreign Affairs, Dr. Édouard Bizimana, issued a decree introducing stricter requirements for Burundians seeking employment abroad. While officially applicable to all citizens, multiple sources say the measure primarily targets military personnel attempting to desert.
Under the new rules, any Burundian departing for work abroad must present an identity card issued by the competent ministry, a signed contract from the employer, and authorization from a family member. For soldiers, this effectively requires documentation from the Ministry of Defense and Veterans Affairs, which is not issued to active-duty personnel.
Previously, Burundi’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs only monitored labor migration to countries that had formal worker-exchange agreements with Burundi. The new directive expands oversight to all destination countries, including those without bilateral agreements.
The move signals a significant tightening of controls as Burundi seeks to curb military desertions amid growing domestic unease over its role in the DRC conflict.

title: DRC - AFC/M23 Accuses Kinshasa of Breaching Peace Agreements
excerpt: Kinshasa/Uvira, January 1, 2026 Corneille Nangaa, coordinator of the AFC/M23, has accused the government of the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) of failing to honor agreements signed in 2025 aimed at stabilizing the eastern region and ensuring the security of Abanye-Congophone
title_en: DRC - AFC/M23 Accuses Kinshasa of Breaching Peace Agreements
excerpt_en: Kinshasa/Uvira, January 1, 2026 Corneille Nangaa, coordinator of the AFC/M23, has accused the government of the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) of failing to honor agreements signed in 2025 aimed at stabilizing the eastern region and ensuring the security of Abanye-Congophone
body_en:
Kinshasa/Uvira, January 1, 2026
Corneille Nangaa, coordinator of the AFC/M23, has accused the government of the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) of failing to honor agreements signed in 2025 aimed at stabilizing the eastern region and ensuring the security of Abanye-Congophone communities.
The agreements, signed in July 2025 under Qatari mediation, included a Declaration of Principles, a prisoner release mechanism, a ceasefire and monitoring mechanism, and a basic framework for peace.
In a recent statement, Nangaa criticized Kinshasa for betraying the trust of the AFC/M23. “The regime of Kinshasa has shown its inability to uphold its commitments and its own word. This is a regime built on lies and outdated agreements. To date, no prisoners have been released, in clear violation of the signed accords,” he said.
He also accused the DRC of ceasefire violations through repeated attacks against AFC/M23 positions.
While acknowledging the peace agreement between Rwanda and the DRC signed in Washington as a positive development, Nangaa emphasized that negotiations in Doha between Kinshasa and AFC/M23 have not yielded concrete results. Several agreements from these talks remain unimplemented.
Despite these setbacks, Nangaa reaffirmed that the AFC/M23 withdrew its forces from the city of Uvira as requested by the mediators, demonstrating continued commitment to peace efforts.

title: AFC/M23 Accuses DRC Government of Genocide Amid Ongoing Violence
excerpt: January 2, 2026 - Eastern DRC The AFC/M23 Alliance has accused the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) government of committing acts of genocide, condemning what it describes as systematic attacks against civilians in the eastern regions of the country. The statement, released on
title_en: AFC/M23 Accuses DRC Government of Genocide Amid Ongoing Violence
excerpt_en: January 2, 2026 - Eastern DRC The AFC/M23 Alliance has accused the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) government of committing acts of genocide, condemning what it describes as systematic attacks against civilians in the eastern regions of the country. The statement, released on
body_en:
January 2, 2026 - Eastern DRC
The AFC/M23 Alliance has accused the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) government of committing acts of genocide, condemning what it describes as systematic attacks against civilians in the eastern regions of the country. The statement, released on January 2, 2026, cites widespread human rights violations, targeting women, and looting by Congolese government forces in areas including Uvira, Makobola, Kamanyola, Luvungi, and Sange.
According to the group, Kamanyola alone saw eight people killed and 55 others injured, while civilians in Uvira faced violent suppression during a peaceful demonstration on December 22, 2025, where heavy weaponry was reportedly used against protesters.
The statement criticized the DRC government under President Félix Tshisekedi, accusing it of prioritizing military expenditures, such as drones, over the protection of civilians in the eastern provinces. AFC/M23 further condemned:
Deliberate violations of the ceasefire agreement
Hate crimes and ethnically motivated torture
Systematic attacks on populated areas and AFC/M23 positions by land, sea, and air
Hate speech propagated by former FARDC Military Spokesperson, Gen Maj Sylvain Ekenge, in an interview aired on RTNC on December 27, 2025
The group emphasized that these actions contravene international principles against genocide, including those adopted in 1948, and constitute a campaign of persecution, exclusion, and oppression against Tutsi communities in the DRC.
AFC/M23 reiterated its commitment to defending those affected, protecting their security, dignity, and fundamental rights, stating:
“We are on the side of those who continue to be oppressed and will continue to make efforts to protect them against this murderous regime.”
The alliance called on the international community to recognize these violations and take notice of the ongoing humanitarian crisis in eastern DRC.

title: AFC/M23 Claims Discovery of Belgian-Supplied Weapons Near Uvira
excerpt: January 3, 2026 - The AFC/M23 movement claims that its fighters discovered a cache of weapons allegedly supplied to the Democratic Republic of Congo by Belgium during their advance toward Uvira, according to statements by Dr. Balinda Oscar, Deputy Spokesperson of the AFC/M23. Dr.
title_en: AFC/M23 Claims Discovery of Belgian-Supplied Weapons Near Uvira
excerpt_en: January 3, 2026 - The AFC/M23 movement claims that its fighters discovered a cache of weapons allegedly supplied to the Democratic Republic of Congo by Belgium during their advance toward Uvira, according to statements by Dr. Balinda Oscar, Deputy Spokesperson of the AFC/M23. Dr.
body_en:
January 3, 2026 - The AFC/M23 movement claims that its fighters discovered a cache of weapons allegedly supplied to the Democratic Republic of Congo by Belgium during their advance toward Uvira, according to statements by Dr. Balinda Oscar, Deputy Spokesperson of the AFC/M23.
Dr. Balinda asserted that, as fighters reached the Luvungi area, less than 10 kilometers from Uvira, they came across military equipment still packed in boxes, allegedly stored in a school and not yet deployed. He claimed the weapons had been provided by Belgium to the DRC.
According to the AFC/M23 official, the capture of Uvira followed what he described as provocations by Congolese forces, including airstrikes in Kamanyola that reportedly caused civilian casualties and property destruction. He alleged that Burundian elements had joined the fighting, prompting the movement to resume hostilities after a period he described as ten months of calm in parts of Kamanyola and Katogota.
Dr. Balinda further claimed that the coalition opposing the AFC/M23 lacked combat experience, alleging that some Wazalendo fighters were civilians without adequate training, and accusing Burundian Imbonerakure of operating in military uniforms.
He also alleged that a significant portion of the AFC/M23’s equipment is obtained from the battlefield, claiming that some FARDC officers abandoned or sold weapons-an assertion he linked to ongoing judicial proceedings against senior officers.
Addressing Belgium’s role, Dr. Balinda accused Brussels of maintaining political and military support for Kinshasa, citing historical ties and what he described as a close relationship with President Félix Tshisekedi. He used strong language to claim that Congolese sovereignty had been compromised, framing the conflict as a renewed struggle for independence.
Despite these accusations, Dr. Balinda stated that the AFC/M23 supports peace talks with the Congolese government and insisted that the movement does not seek to seize power, but claims to be fighting for the rights of the Congolese people.

title: More Than 1,000 Burundian Soldiers Missing Over the Past Month
excerpt: More than 1,000 Burundian soldiers deployed in the Rusizi/Ruzizi Valley in the eastern Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) have gone missing over the past month. Between December 2 and 9, 2025, intense fighting erupted in several areas, including Luvungi, Sange, Luberizi, and Kili
title_en: More Than 1,000 Burundian Soldiers Missing Over the Past Month
excerpt_en: More than 1,000 Burundian soldiers deployed in the Rusizi/Ruzizi Valley in the eastern Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) have gone missing over the past month. Between December 2 and 9, 2025, intense fighting erupted in several areas, including Luvungi, Sange, Luberizi, and Kili
body_en:
More than 1,000 Burundian soldiers deployed in the Rusizi/Ruzizi Valley in the eastern Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) have gone missing over the past month. Between December 2 and 9, 2025, intense fighting erupted in several areas, including Luvungi, Sange, Luberizi, and Kiliba, pitting M23 fighters against DRC forces, supported by Burundian troops, the Wazalendo movement, and the FDLR.
The clashes began with the deployment of approximately 20,000 Burundian soldiers in South Kivu province. During the fighting, Burundian forces reportedly suffered heavy losses, including soldiers killed, wounded, or captured. The injured were evacuated to medical facilities such as Kamenge Military Hospital, Tanganyika Care Polyclinic, and Kira Hospital.
The M23 movement has confirmed that it captured numerous Burundian soldiers during the fighting in the Rusizi Valley, stating that it is respecting their rights while in custody and expressing its intention to facilitate their return home. Although M23 has not disclosed exact figures, sources in South Kivu indicate that the number of captured soldiers runs into the hundreds.
On January 4, 2026, the FOCODE organization, which advocates for the rights of Burundians, particularly those who have disappeared, announced that more than 1,000 Burundian soldiers are unaccounted for in the Rusizi Valley. Their status remains unclear, with uncertainty over whether they are alive, captured, killed, or wandering in the forests.
According to testimonies from soldiers who participated in the fighting in Kamanyola-Lubarika-Luvungi, the Burundian army has no information on the whereabouts of over 1,000 soldiers. It is reportedly unknown whether they died in combat, deserted, were captured, or remain missing in the bush.
Another reliable source in Burundi claims that 1,794 Burundian soldiers lost their lives in the Rusizi Valley, adding that these soldiers are considered to have deserted the army, with their whereabouts still unknown.

title: Conflict Erupts Between Wazalendo and FARDC Leadership
excerpt: On January 7, 2026, tensions surfaced between the Wazalendo coalition, aligned with the Congolese government, and the Democratic Republic of Congo’s military leadership. According to Wazalendo spokesperson Habyarimana Mbitsemunda, also known as Jules Mulumba, a serious conspiracy
title_en: Conflict Erupts Between Wazalendo and FARDC Leadership
excerpt_en: On January 7, 2026, tensions surfaced between the Wazalendo coalition, aligned with the Congolese government, and the Democratic Republic of Congo’s military leadership. According to Wazalendo spokesperson Habyarimana Mbitsemunda, also known as Jules Mulumba, a serious conspiracy
body_en:
On January 7, 2026, tensions surfaced between the Wazalendo coalition, aligned with the Congolese government, and the Democratic Republic of Congo’s military leadership. According to Wazalendo spokesperson Habyarimana Mbitsemunda, also known as Jules Mulumba, a serious conspiracy within the FARDC affected battlefield operations and internal coordination.
Mulumba stated that the arrest of Gen. Maj. Janvier Mayanga wa Gishuba, Deputy Commander of the DRC’s Rescue Forces, was the result of a conspiracy orchestrated by Lt. Gen. Padiri Bulenda, the FARDC Commander-in-Chief. He explained that Gen. Mayanga opposed the transfer of $8 million intended for Wazalendo from the Ministry of Defense and Finance.
The Wazalendo leadership also criticized Lt. Gen. Padiri Bulenda for sending messages attacking their coalition, which Mulumba described as a smear campaign against these armed groups. Mulumba further accused Gen. Fall Sikabwe of contributing to the capture of Goma by AFC/M23 forces on January 27, 2025, alleging that he facilitated joint operations between South African, Burundian, and Wazalendo forces.
Other FARDC officers were also blamed for military failures. Mulumba cited Lt. Gen. Masunzu Pacifique and Brig. Gen. Olivier Gasita, both from South Kivu, as responsible for operational missteps, questioning why they remain in active positions.
In Kinshasa, several senior officers were arrested over alleged plots against President Félix Tshisekedi, including Gen. Dieudonné Mutupeke Kiamata, Gen. Marcel Mbangu Mashita, Gen. Franck Ntumba (formerly in charge of military operations at the presidential palace), and Gen. Christian Tshiwewe Songesha, Chief of Army Staff. Wazalendo claims that Gen. Ntumba and Gen. Tshiwewe were involved in planning a coup, while Mutupeke and Mbangu face accusations of crimes they did not commit.
This dispute highlights deep fractures within the Congolese military and its allied forces, revealing mistrust and infighting that continue to undermine security operations in eastern DRC.

Fall Sikabwe of contributing to the capture of Goma by AFC/M23 forces on January 27, 2025, alleging that he facilitated joint operations between South African, Burundian, and Wazalendo forces.
Other FARDC officers were also blamed for military failures. Mulumba cited Lt. Gen. Masunzu Pacifique and Brig. Gen. Olivier Gasita, both from South Kivu, as responsible for operational missteps, questioning why they remain in active positions.
In Kinshasa, several senior officers were arrested over alleged plots against President Félix Tshisekedi, including Gen. Dieudonné Mutupeke Kiamata, Gen. Marcel Mbangu Mashita, Gen. Franck Ntumba (formerly in charge of military operations at the presidential palace), and Gen. Christian Tshiwewe Songesha, Chief of Army Staff. Wazalendo claims that Gen. Ntumba and Gen. Tshiwewe were involved in planning a coup, while Mutupeke and Mbangu face accusations of crimes they did not commit.
This dispute highlights deep fractures within the Congolese military and its allied forces, revealing mistrust and infighting that continue to undermine security operations in eastern DRC.

body_en:
Goma, 8 January 2026: The AFC/M23 rebel coalition has issued a direct threat against President Félix Tshisekedi Tshilombo, announcing intentions to arrest him and bring him to court.
The statement came from Lt Col Willy Ngoma, spokesman for AFC/M23, during a farewell ceremony for 22 civilians from the Masisi Center, North Kivu, who were reportedly killed by a DRC Army drone strike on 2 January 2026.
Lt Col Ngoma said: "He will definitely pay for this. It will not be long, you will see. He will go to court for these things. We will arrest him, he will go to court."
The General Director of AFC/M23, Corneille Nangaa, condemned the DRC government for killing civilians, accusing it of failing to distinguish between combatants and non-combatants. He stated: "The false political power that the Kinshasa government has given itself does not give it the right to kill civilians. No elections, no international recognition, no patriotic struggle can justify the killing of civilians."
Nangaa assured residents in AFC/M23-controlled areas that their security remains a priority, promising that the fighters will continue to protect civilians with the same dedication.
This latest declaration underscores the rising tensions between the DRC government and the AFC/M23, with threats now extending directly to the national leadership.

title: Burundi Sends Troops Back to Fizi Amid Alleged Threats to Banyamulenge Civilians
excerpt: Fizi, DRC - 8 January 2026: Burundi has redeployed troops to areas inhabited by the Banyamulenge in the Democratic Republic of Congo, prompting condemnation from the armed group MRDP-Twirwaneho, which opposes the DRC government. According to Col Kamasa Ndakize Welcome, spokesman
title_en: Burundi Sends Troops Back to Fizi Amid Alleged Threats to Banyamulenge Civilians
excerpt_en: Fizi, DRC - 8 January 2026: Burundi has redeployed troops to areas inhabited by the Banyamulenge in the Democratic Republic of Congo, prompting condemnation from the armed group MRDP-Twirwaneho, which opposes the DRC government. According to Col Kamasa Ndakize Welcome, spokesman
body_en:
Fizi, DRC - 8 January 2026: Burundi has redeployed troops to areas inhabited by the Banyamulenge in the Democratic Republic of Congo, prompting condemnation from the armed group MRDP-Twirwaneho, which opposes the DRC government.
According to Col Kamasa Ndakize Welcome, spokesman for Twirwaneho, Burundian forces, led by officers including one named Nshimirimana, returned to the Bibokoboko and Point-Zéro areas with intentions to control the mountainous region.
He said: "MRDP-Twirwaneho strongly condemns this evil plan of foreign forces, which only aims to attack Banyamulenge civilians in Bibokoboko and Minembwe and block their access, which will make their situation worse."
MRDP-Twirwaneho claimed that since March 2025, Burundian troops, collaborating with the DRC government, Wazalendo groups, and FDLR forces, have reportedly killed and tortured civilians, abducted individuals, committed sexual violence, and looted property.
Since October 2025, the Banyamulenge in Minembwe have faced worsening conditions, with blocked roads to markets and health centers, causing shortages of basic goods and a spike in deaths, particularly among children under five due to lack of medical care.
After the AFC/M23 coalition captured Uvira and much of the Ruzizi Valley in December 2025, many Burundian troops temporarily returned home. Recent reports indicate that they have now redeployed to Fizi, including the town of Baraka, to resume joint operations with DRC forces.
MRDP-Twirwaneho warned that it will not tolerate the presence of these troops while civilian security and property remain at risk.
This development highlights the ongoing regional complexities in eastern DRC, with foreign forces and local militias continuing to impact the safety and livelihood of vulnerable communities.

title: Angolan President Lourenço Urges DRC Government and AFC/M23 to End Hostilities
excerpt: Luanda, Angola - 8 January 2026: Angolan President and African Union Chairperson, João Lourenço, has called on the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) government and the AFC/M23 coalition to immediately cease hostilities and focus on a peaceful resolution to the ongoing conflict i
title_en: Angolan President Lourenço Urges DRC Government and AFC/M23 to End Hostilities
excerpt_en: Luanda, Angola - 8 January 2026: Angolan President and African Union Chairperson, João Lourenço, has called on the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) government and the AFC/M23 coalition to immediately cease hostilities and focus on a peaceful resolution to the ongoing conflict i
body_en:
Luanda, Angola - 8 January 2026: Angolan President and African Union Chairperson, João Lourenço, has called on the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) government and the AFC/M23 coalition to immediately cease hostilities and focus on a peaceful resolution to the ongoing conflict in eastern DRC.
President Lourenço made the statement following a meeting with DRC President Félix Tshisekedi, who traveled to Luanda to discuss strategies to restore peace and security in the region.
Expressing concern over the continued instability and displacement in eastern DRC, Lourenço warned that ongoing fighting is undermining international peace initiatives, including talks previously held in Washington and Doha.
He urged all parties to:
Cease hostilities immediately
Respect existing agreements
Prioritize the interests of the Congolese people Lourenço also called on the international community to support efforts aimed at stabilizing eastern DRC.
Tshisekedi has requested that new peace talks bring together representatives from all Congolese groups, including the AFC/M23, with discussions to be held in Kinshasa under the facilitation of the Angolan government.
According to reports, Lourenço has accepted Tshisekedi’s request, engaging with opposition figures in the DRC to prepare for the talks. Tshisekedi emphasized that the AFC/M23 must first observe a ceasefire, while the DRC government will verify compliance before formal negotiations begin.
This development signals renewed efforts to restart dialogue in the eastern DRC conflict, with Angola taking a central mediation role.

title: Renewed Clashes in Masisi: AFC/M23 and Wazalendo Battle Amid Civilian Casualties
excerpt: Masisi, North Kivu - 11 January 2026: Fighting has resumed in Masisi Territory between the AFC/M23 rebels and the Wazalendo coalition, aligned with the DRC government. According to local reports, clashes began at midnight in the Kazinga area, with residents hearing heavy and ligh
title_en: Renewed Clashes in Masisi: AFC/M23 and Wazalendo Battle Amid Civilian Casualties
excerpt_en: Masisi, North Kivu - 11 January 2026: Fighting has resumed in Masisi Territory between the AFC/M23 rebels and the Wazalendo coalition, aligned with the DRC government. According to local reports, clashes began at midnight in the Kazinga area, with residents hearing heavy and ligh
body_en:
Masisi, North Kivu - 11 January 2026: Fighting has resumed in Masisi Territory between the AFC/M23 rebels and the Wazalendo coalition, aligned with the DRC government. According to local reports, clashes began at midnight in the Kazinga area, with residents hearing heavy and light weapons being fired.
Sources say the Wazalendo forces are attempting to prevent AFC/M23 from expanding control over additional areas, including the first and second Nyamaboko groups.
This flare-up follows a FARDC attack on 2 January 2026, during which six civilians were killed and 41 others injured in a populated area of Masisi. Both AFC/M23 and the United Nations peacekeeping mission (MONUSCO) condemned the January 2 attack.
The renewed clashes highlight the ongoing instability in North Kivu, where armed confrontations continue to threaten civilians and hamper peace efforts in the region.
Conclusion
Between late 2025 and early 2026, Rwanda and the surrounding region are characterized by a dual focus on internal development and complex regional diplomacy. Internally, Rwanda is experiencing significant growth in private investment and infrastructure, exemplified by the inauguration of the 7 billion Frw GLADS Apartment and the expansion of the Karenge Waterworks to meet increasing demand for clean water. The government is also modernizing economic services through initiatives like the Rwanda Development Board’s One Stop Center website to further streamline investment.
On the diplomatic and security front, the period is marked by several key developments:
Regional Influence and Cooperation: Rwanda continues to be viewed as a model for peacebuilding, with nations like Sudan actively seeking its expertise for national reconstruction. Furthermore, Rwandan peacekeepers continue to receive international recognition for their professionalism in missions like MINUSCA in the Central African Republic.
Ongoing DRC Tensions: Relations between Rwanda and the Democratic Republic of the Congo remain strained. The DRC government faces internal and external criticism for its handling of security in the East, with ongoing conflicts involving the AFC/M23 coalition. While there are shifting efforts to restart mediation-moving between Qatari-led and Angolan-led frameworks-the path to a lasting peace remains uncertain due to deep-seated mistrust and conflicting negotiation strategies.
Strategic Resource Management: Rwanda is proactively addressing future challenges, such as the need to expand its national fuel reserves to accommodate rising consumption driven by industrial growth and increased vehicle use.
In summary, while Rwanda is successfully advancing its domestic economic and developmental agenda, it remains deeply involved in-and affected by-the persistent security challenges and diplomatic maneuvering in the broader Great Lakes Region.
By Jeff Buleli

title: Rwanda and Oman Sign Four Strategic Cooperation Agreements
excerpt: Kigali/Muscat, January 12, 2026 - Rwanda and the Sultanate of Oman on Monday signed four cooperation agreements aimed at strengthening bilateral ties across key sectors, including transport, technology, and innovation, the Omani government announced. The agreements were concluded
title_en: Rwanda and Oman Sign Four Strategic Cooperation Agreements
excerpt_en: Kigali/Muscat, January 12, 2026 - Rwanda and the Sultanate of Oman on Monday signed four cooperation agreements aimed at strengthening bilateral ties across key sectors, including transport, technology, and innovation, the Omani government announced. The agreements were concluded
body_en:
Kigali/Muscat, January 12, 2026 - Rwanda and the Sultanate of Oman on Monday signed four cooperation agreements aimed at strengthening bilateral ties across key sectors, including transport, technology, and innovation, the Omani government announced.
The agreements were concluded following an official visit by a high-level Rwandan delegation to Oman, led by the Minister of Foreign Affairs and International Cooperation, Amb. Olivier Nduhungirehe. The delegation also included the Minister of Technology and Innovation, Paula Ingabire, the Minister of Finance and Economic Planning, Yusuf Murangwa, and the State Minister for Infrastructure at the Ministry of Infrastructure, Eng. Jean de Dieu Uwihanganye.
According to Omani authorities, the accords focus on enhancing cooperation in land ports and freight transport, with both countries set to benefit from joint initiatives aimed at developing logistics and trade infrastructure.
Additional agreements cover the establishment of a large data warehouse, the development of IT infrastructure, and collaboration on projects related to artificial intelligence. Under these frameworks, Rwanda and Oman will jointly build capacity, share expertise, and develop strategies and regulatory frameworks to advance technological innovation.
A separate agreement on air transport will see Oman Air launch direct flights to Kigali starting in June 2026. The airline will operate two non-stop flights per week, marking a significant step in improving connectivity between the two countries.
The fourth agreement, signed between the Rwanda Development Board (RDB) and Oman Airports Company, focuses on air transport development through joint investments, infrastructure development, and the exchange of technical expertise.
Speaking after the signing ceremony, Amb. Nduhungirehe described the agreements as a major milestone in Rwanda-Oman relations, emphasizing their tangible benefits for citizens of both nations.
“Rwanda and Oman share geographical and strategic links through the Indian Ocean, particularly as Rwanda is a member of the East African Community,” he said. “We are committed to implementing these agreements and to signing more in the coming days, all with the goal of delivering real benefits to our people.”
Oman’s Minister of Transport, Communications and Information Technology, Eng. Saeed bin Hamoud Al Maawali, said the agreements align with Oman’s broader strategy to expand cooperation with East Africa.
He added that the accords not only reinforce the strong bilateral relations between Rwanda and Oman but also contribute to shaping a wider framework for cooperation between the Middle East and Africa.

A separate agreement on air transport will see Oman Air launch direct flights to Kigali starting in June 2026. The airline will operate two non-stop flights per week, marking a significant step in improving connectivity between the two countries.
The fourth agreement, signed between the Rwanda Development Board (RDB) and Oman Airports Company, focuses on air transport development through joint investments, infrastructure development, and the exchange of technical expertise.
Speaking after the signing ceremony, Amb. Nduhungirehe described the agreements as a major milestone in Rwanda-Oman relations, emphasizing their tangible benefits for citizens of both nations.
“Rwanda and Oman share geographical and strategic links through the Indian Ocean, particularly as Rwanda is a member of the East African Community,” he said. “We are committed to implementing these agreements and to signing more in the coming days, all with the goal of delivering real benefits to our people.”
Oman’s Minister of Transport, Communications and Information Technology, Eng. Saeed bin Hamoud Al Maawali, said the agreements align with Oman’s broader strategy to expand cooperation with East Africa.
He added that the accords not only reinforce the strong bilateral relations between Rwanda and Oman but also contribute to shaping a wider framework for cooperation between the Middle East and Africa.

body_en:
Kinshasa/Luanda, January 13, 2026 - The Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) government has been placed on high alert following the entry of AFC/M23 fighters into the city of Uvira on December 10, 2025, amid fears that Kalemie in Tanganyika Province could also fall.
In response to the situation, Kinshasa sought military assistance from several countries to counter the rebel advance. In mid-December, the DRC formally requested support from Angola, citing Luanda’s role as a guarantor of President Félix Tshisekedi’s political stability.
However, Angolan authorities rejected the request to deploy troops, recalling that Angola had not intervened militarily even when regional forces were previously deployed to North Kivu Province.
On December 14, 2025, President Tshisekedi traveled to Luanda, where Angolan President and African Union Chairperson João Lourenço expressed support for a political solution rather than a military one.
Tshisekedi returned to Luanda on January 5, 2026, where both leaders agreed on the need for inclusive dialogue involving Congolese stakeholders from different sectors, including opposition figures and armed groups such as the AFC/M23. The Congolese president proposed that the talks be held in Kinshasa.
At Tshisekedi’s request, President Lourenço has continued consultations with potential participants. Former President Joseph Kabila and his close associates, including Moïse Nyarugabo and Raymond Tshibanda, were recently reported to be in Luanda as part of these discussions.
Despite clear signs that a new peace process is underway, both the Congolese and Angolan governments have avoided formally labeling the initiative as “new peace talks.”
AFC/M23 leader Corneille Nangaa has asked President Lourenço to clarify how the proposed process differs from the previous Doha talks, particularly after the group was invited to Luanda to prepare for discussions scheduled in Kinshasa.
On January 8, 2026, President Tshisekedi returned once again to Luanda to continue talks with Lourenço after agreeing on a list of potential participants for the upcoming dialogue.

title: Burundi Faces Power Struggle Between President Ndayishimiye and CNDD-FDD Leader Ndikuriyo
excerpt: Bujumbura, January 14, 2026 - Burundi is witnessing a renewed struggle for political power between President Évariste Ndayishimiye and Révérien Ndikuriyo, Secretary General of the ruling CNDD-FDD party. Recent statements by Ndikuriyo have fueled speculation over who truly holds a
title_en: Burundi Faces Power Struggle Between President Ndayishimiye and CNDD-FDD Leader Ndikuriyo
excerpt_en: Bujumbura, January 14, 2026 - Burundi is witnessing a renewed struggle for political power between President Évariste Ndayishimiye and Révérien Ndikuriyo, Secretary General of the ruling CNDD-FDD party. Recent statements by Ndikuriyo have fueled speculation over who truly holds a
body_en:
Bujumbura, January 14, 2026 - Burundi is witnessing a renewed struggle for political power between President Évariste Ndayishimiye and Révérien Ndikuriyo, Secretary General of the ruling CNDD-FDD party. Recent statements by Ndikuriyo have fueled speculation over who truly holds authority in the country.
At a press conference on January 2, Ndikuriyo suggested that his influence in Burundi rivals, or even surpasses, that of the president, signaling a shift in internal party dynamics. Observers note that Ndikuriyo has increasingly criticized senior government officials, refuted economic claims, and asserted control over key national decisions, including border management with the Democratic Republic of Congo and Rwanda.
He publicly challenged the Minister of Finance, Alain Ndikumana, over alleged security threats involving a fertilizer company, and contradicted government assurances on petroleum shortages, stating the problem would persist until at least 2029. These statements contrast with President Ndayishimiye’s assurances that mining and other resources would strengthen the economy.
Political analysts highlight that tension escalated over control of the National Assembly leadership. Ndayishimiye opposed Daniel Gélase Ndabirabe continuing as head of deputies, while Ndikuriyo and CNDD-FDD leaders insisted he remain. This disagreement extended to cabinet formation, with Ndayishimiye appointing ministers loyal to him, including in defense, security, justice, foreign affairs, and finance. Ndikuriyo publicly rejects the legitimacy of this government, further demonstrating the power divide.
The ongoing military challenges in eastern DRC have also weakened Ndayishimiye’s perceived authority, bolstering Ndikuriyo’s position within the party. Analysts note that while both leaders share ideological goals-opposing foreign exploitation and criticizing government institutions-their methods and influence are sharply contested.
Historically, the CNDD-FDD has experienced recurring internal conflicts, including power struggles under former President Pierre Nkurunziza between 2005 and 2010. Ndikuriyo’s assertiveness reflects a continuation of this pattern, where political authority is often enforced through loyalty, intimidation, or the marginalization of rivals.
Despite Ndayishimiye’s public warnings to government staff about dual allegiances, observers question his ultimate ability to enforce authority over CNDD-FDD’s powerful party structures. The current power struggle underscores the fragility of institutional governance in Burundi and the enduring influence of party leadership over state affairs.

title: EAC Deploys Observers to Monitor Uganda Elections, Led by Edda Mukabagwiza
excerpt: Kigali/Kampala, January 13, 2026 - Rwandan lawyer and diplomat Edda Mukabagwiza has been appointed to lead the East African Community (EAC) observer mission for Uganda’s upcoming presidential and parliamentary elections scheduled for January 15, 2026. On January 13, the EAC deplo
title_en: EAC Deploys Observers to Monitor Uganda Elections, Led by Edda Mukabagwiza
excerpt_en: Kigali/Kampala, January 13, 2026 - Rwandan lawyer and diplomat Edda Mukabagwiza has been appointed to lead the East African Community (EAC) observer mission for Uganda’s upcoming presidential and parliamentary elections scheduled for January 15, 2026. On January 13, the EAC deplo
body_en:
Kigali/Kampala, January 13, 2026 - Rwandan lawyer and diplomat Edda Mukabagwiza has been appointed to lead the East African Community (EAC) observer mission for Uganda’s upcoming presidential and parliamentary elections scheduled for January 15, 2026.
On January 13, the EAC deployed 61 observers from across its member states to monitor the electoral process. The team includes members of the EAC Assembly, national electoral commissions, foreign affairs ministries, human rights commissions, civil society organizations, and the EAC Secretariat.
Mukabagwiza, whose extensive experience includes serving as Deputy Speaker of the Rwandan Parliament, Minister of Justice, ambassador to multiple countries, and a practicing lawyer, emphasized the mission’s independence and impartiality.
“We are not here to interfere in the electoral process, approve political outcomes, or announce results,” Mukabagwiza said. “Our mission is to observe objectively, collect accurate information, and report impartially.”
Observers will be stationed across Uganda, engaging with the Electoral Commission, political parties, candidates, civil society, media, security agencies, and other stakeholders to monitor the elections comprehensively.
Following the polls, the EAC team is expected to issue an interim report on the conduct of the elections, followed by a final report submitted to the EAC Council of Ministers, the Ugandan government, and other stakeholders. The reports will include recommendations to strengthen future electoral processes and ensure transparency and fairness.

title: 15 January 2026; Rwanda and Luxembourg Discuss Financial Cooperation
excerpt: Rwandan Ambassador to Luxembourg, Munyangaju Aurore Mimosa, has held discussions with Luxembourg’s Minister of Finance, Gilles Roth, on strengthening financial cooperation between the two countries. In a statement, Ambassador Munyangaju said the talks focused on deepening bilater
title_en: 15 January 2026; Rwanda and Luxembourg Discuss Financial Cooperation
excerpt_en: Rwandan Ambassador to Luxembourg, Munyangaju Aurore Mimosa, has held discussions with Luxembourg’s Minister of Finance, Gilles Roth, on strengthening financial cooperation between the two countries. In a statement, Ambassador Munyangaju said the talks focused on deepening bilater
body_en:
Rwandan Ambassador to Luxembourg, Munyangaju Aurore Mimosa, has held discussions with Luxembourg’s Minister of Finance, Gilles Roth, on strengthening financial cooperation between the two countries.
In a statement, Ambassador Munyangaju said the talks focused on deepening bilateral financial ties and reinforcing the strong partnership between Rwanda and Luxembourg.
Ambassador Munyangaju arrived in Luxembourg on February 25, 2025, and officially presented her credentials on March 20, 2025.
The two countries already maintain strong cooperation. In 2024, the governments of Rwanda and Luxembourg signed a €12 million funding agreement to address the impacts of climate change.
In October 2021, both countries also signed a cooperation agreement aimed at promoting the development of the Kigali International Financial Centre, particularly in human resource development, operational capacity building, and positioning the center at an international level.
Rwanda and Luxembourg further cooperate through agreements targeting anti-smuggling efforts and tax evasion prevention.

title: Ambassador Gen. Maj. Nzabamwita Presents Credentials to President Putin
excerpt: Rwanda’s Ambassador to the Russian Federation, Gen. Maj. Joseph Nzabamwita, has formally presented his credentials to President Vladimir Putin, conveying a message from President Paul Kagame. The ceremony took place at the Kremlin Presidential Palace on January 15, 2026, alongsid
title_en: Ambassador Gen. Maj. Nzabamwita Presents Credentials to President Putin
excerpt_en: Rwanda’s Ambassador to the Russian Federation, Gen. Maj. Joseph Nzabamwita, has formally presented his credentials to President Vladimir Putin, conveying a message from President Paul Kagame. The ceremony took place at the Kremlin Presidential Palace on January 15, 2026, alongsid
body_en:
Rwanda’s Ambassador to the Russian Federation, Gen. Maj. Joseph Nzabamwita, has formally presented his credentials to President Vladimir Putin, conveying a message from President Paul Kagame.
The ceremony took place at the Kremlin Presidential Palace on January 15, 2026, alongside 31 other ambassadors accredited to Russia. Senior Russian officials in attendance included Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov and Head of the Presidential Administration Yuri Ushakov.
Ambassador Nzabamwita officially assumed his duties on April 22, 2025, after presenting copies of his credentials to Deputy Foreign Minister Mikhail Bogdanov. He succeeds Lt. Gen. (Rtd) Frank Mushyo Kamanzi, who concluded his mission on February 4, 2024.
In his address, President Putin underscored that Russia’s foreign policy is grounded in mutual respect, adherence to international law, and the promotion of inclusive governance. He reaffirmed the importance of Russia’s relations with Africa, describing them as based on mutually beneficial cooperation.
“A large number of ambassadors from friendly African countries are present today, including representatives from Rwanda, Somalia, Gabon, Senegal, Mauritania, Algeria, Ghana, and Namibia,” President Putin said. “Russia maintains constructive relations with all African countries through cooperation, assistance, and partnership. We are committed to expanding political, economic, and humanitarian ties.”
He recalled Russia’s historical role in supporting African countries’ paths to independence and development, and noted ongoing commitments made during the Russia-Africa Summits in Sochi and Saint Petersburg, as well as the Africa-Russia Foreign Ministers’ Summit held in Cairo in 2025, with another summit planned for this year.
Following the ceremony, Ambassador Nzabamwita delivered President Kagame’s message to President Putin and held separate discussions with Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov and Yuri Ushakov, reaffirming their commitment to sustained dialogue.
The talks focused on strengthening the longstanding relations between Rwanda and Russia, which date back to 1963 and have steadily expanded over the years. Presidents Kagame and Putin previously held bilateral discussions during the Russia-Africa Summits in 2018 and 2019.
Bilateral cooperation continues to grow in several sectors, including nuclear technology, where Russia is supporting Rwanda’s efforts to develop nuclear energy, and education, with hundreds of Rwandan students currently studying at Russian universities.
The Rwandan Embassy in Russia reiterated its commitment to deepening these ties and expanding cooperation across the political, economic, social, cultural, commercial, and tourism sectors.

title: Ndayishimiye Denies Burundi’s Role in DRC War
excerpt: January 17, 2026 - Burundian President Évariste Ndayishimiye has denied his country’s involvement in the war in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), presenting himself as a key actor in efforts to restore peace and reconciliation in the region. Since 2022, the Burundian go
title_en: Ndayishimiye Denies Burundi’s Role in DRC War
excerpt_en: January 17, 2026 - Burundian President Évariste Ndayishimiye has denied his country’s involvement in the war in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), presenting himself as a key actor in efforts to restore peace and reconciliation in the region. Since 2022, the Burundian go
body_en:
January 17, 2026 - Burundian President Évariste Ndayishimiye has denied his country’s involvement in the war in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), presenting himself as a key actor in efforts to restore peace and reconciliation in the region.
Since 2022, the Burundian government has deployed troops to eastern DRC under a bilateral agreement aimed at combating armed groups, including RED Tabara and M23. Burundian forces reportedly suffered heavy losses in North Kivu Province before withdrawing toward South Kivu, where M23 later seized key cities, including Bukavu and Uvira.
Speaking to diplomats in Burundi, Ndayishimiye said he played a major role last year in resolving the conflict, despite widespread perceptions that his country was directly involved in the fighting.
“No, Burundi is not at war. Burundi went to help the DRC to protect the security of its people. We did not go to war. That is why we continue to do our best to play a role in reconciliation, so that the region can find peace,” he said.
He further claimed that the arrival of the Burundian army in South Kivu helped unite previously divided communities, including the Banyamulenge, Bembe, and Fulero.
“You have seen that when the Burundian army arrived in South Kivu, the Banyamulenge, the Bembe, and the Fulero who were fighting immediately united... In South Kivu, we united everyone, and now I am happy that everyone is sending me messages of gratitude,” he said.
However, despite these claims, reports indicate that in 2025, the Burundian army launched major attacks on the Banyamulenge in Minembwe, in collaboration with the DRC government, Wazalendo groups - including Ababembe and Abafulero - and the FDLR terrorist group.
In October 2025, Burundian forces reportedly blocked all roads connecting Minembwe commune to other parts of South Kivu Province, restricting access to markets and health services, citing the presence of the MRDP-Twirwaneho group.
After the AFC/M23 captured Uvira on December 9, Burundian military operations in the DRC were temporarily disrupted. However, attacks have since resumed on Minembwe and surrounding areas where Banyamulenge communities have sought refuge, in coordination with DRC and Wazalendo forces.

title: Rwanda Urges Regional Talks to Uphold Washington Accords
excerpt: Kigali, January 17, 2026 - Rwanda has called for regional security talks to build on the Washington Accords, emphasizing that ongoing peace efforts in the Great Lakes Region should not ignore the diplomatic progress achieved in 2025. Foreign Minister Olivier Nduhungirehe made the
title_en: Rwanda Urges Regional Talks to Uphold Washington Accords
excerpt_en: Kigali, January 17, 2026 - Rwanda has called for regional security talks to build on the Washington Accords, emphasizing that ongoing peace efforts in the Great Lakes Region should not ignore the diplomatic progress achieved in 2025. Foreign Minister Olivier Nduhungirehe made the
body_en:
Kigali, January 17, 2026 - Rwanda has called for regional security talks to build on the Washington Accords, emphasizing that ongoing peace efforts in the Great Lakes Region should not ignore the diplomatic progress achieved in 2025.
Foreign Minister Olivier Nduhungirehe made the remarks during a high-level dialogue aimed at strengthening African responses to insecurity in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) and the wider Great Lakes Region. The meeting was held in Togo and chaired by President Faure Essozimna Gnassingbé.
Minister Nduhungirehe stressed that future negotiations must respect the steps taken in 2025, including the peace agreement signed on December 4 in Washington.
“At the beginning of 2026, it is important to emphasize that the diplomatic achievements of 2025 must not be undermined and should be preserved. Rwanda hopes that today’s talks will help strengthen the African Union’s coordination mechanism, and support the actions of Washington and Doha,” he said.
The peace agreement between Rwanda and the DRC focuses on dismantling the FDLR terrorist group, which has threatened regional security for years, removing Rwanda’s security measures, and facilitating the repatriation of refugees.
It also includes cooperation in infrastructure, park conservation, healthcare, mining, and other development sectors.

title: Museveni Addresses Supporters After Seventh-Term Victory
excerpt: Kampala, January 18, 2026 - After being re-elected to a seventh term, President Yoweri Kaguta Museveni told his rivals that they were fortunate that over 10 million of his supporters did not vote, suggesting that otherwise they would have been deeply ashamed. Uganda’s presidentia
title_en: Museveni Addresses Supporters After Seventh-Term Victory
excerpt_en: Kampala, January 18, 2026 - After being re-elected to a seventh term, President Yoweri Kaguta Museveni told his rivals that they were fortunate that over 10 million of his supporters did not vote, suggesting that otherwise they would have been deeply ashamed. Uganda’s presidentia
body_en:
Kampala, January 18, 2026 - After being re-elected to a seventh term, President Yoweri Kaguta Museveni told his rivals that they were fortunate that over 10 million of his supporters did not vote, suggesting that otherwise they would have been deeply ashamed.
Uganda’s presidential election, held on January 15, 2026, saw Museveni win with 71.6% of the vote, defeating seven other candidates.
Robert Kyagulanyi Ssentamu, popularly known as Bobi Wine, came second with 24.72%.
The Electoral Commission reported that out of 21.6 million registered voters, 52.5% participated.
A total of 11,090,848 votes were counted from 50,739 polling stations nationwide. Museveni received 7,946,772 votes, Bobi Wine 2,741,238, and Mafabi 209,039.
Speaking on his victory, Museveni said, “10 million of my people did not vote. If they had, you would have been deeply ashamed. We got eight million votes, but remember that when we checked the membership, we had 21 million members, over 18 million of whom were eligible to vote.”
Museveni accused the opposition of exploiting the population, alleging that they received foreign money to bribe voters.
“You know that bribe - 10,000 Ugandan shillings for each person. What can 10,000 buy? A fish? A chicken? This is an insult,” he said.
He added that such practices reflect poverty, which must be eradicated to prevent such behavior.
Museveni also praised the Ugandan people, including members of the opposition NUP party led by Bobi Wine, for refusing to join protests.
“There are many NUP members among them. I thank Ugandans. Many came to me and said, ‘We do not want our country to be like Libya. To all you traitors, this is my free advice: stop what you are doing. We know all about you. No matter what, we will fight for peace in Uganda by all means,’” he said.
The 2026 elections differed from those of 2021, as Museveni’s vote total increased, while the number of registered voters also rose by over three million, with a turnout of 59.35%.
In 2021, Museveni received 6,042,898 votes (58.38%), while Bobi Wine came second with 35.08%. Out of 11 candidates, the last received 0.15%.

title: Prof. Tombola Says Lomé Talks Allow Tshisekedi to Evade Previous Agreements
excerpt: Kinshasa, January 19, 2026 - Researcher and university lecturer Prof. Tombola Gustave has criticized the launch of new peace talks on insecurity in eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), arguing that they serve as a way for President Félix Tshisekedi to avoid implementin
title_en: Prof. Tombola Says Lomé Talks Allow Tshisekedi to Evade Previous Agreements
excerpt_en: Kinshasa, January 19, 2026 - Researcher and university lecturer Prof. Tombola Gustave has criticized the launch of new peace talks on insecurity in eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), arguing that they serve as a way for President Félix Tshisekedi to avoid implementin
body_en:
Kinshasa, January 19, 2026 - Researcher and university lecturer Prof. Tombola Gustave has criticized the launch of new peace talks on insecurity in eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), arguing that they serve as a way for President Félix Tshisekedi to avoid implementing previously signed agreements.
The talks, held in Lomé, the capital of Togo, on January 17, 2026, aimed to strengthen African responses to insecurity in the DRC and the Great Lakes Region.
They brought together former heads of state from five African countries and were led by President Faure Essozimna Gnassingbé, who currently chairs the African Union (AU), alongside representatives of the East African Community (EAC), the Southern African Development Community (SADC), and the Chairperson of the AU Commission, Mahmoud Ali Youssouf.
In an interview on National Television, Prof. Tombola acknowledged that the involvement of the AU Chairperson could be seen as an African approach to conflict resolution.
However, he noted that the AU already had an established framework addressing insecurity in eastern DRC, and pointed out that President Tshisekedi personally traveled to Togo, indicating that he had requested the talks.
“Tshisekedi went to Lomé, although no one knows exactly what he said there. That is when it was announced that the DRC issue was now in the hands of the AU and that President Faure was the mediator,” Tombola said. “He went and told him, ‘You have taken matters into your own hands.’”
The researcher recalled that peace efforts under Tshisekedi have followed a long and complex trajectory. He said the president initially attempted dialogue with the AFC/M23, which the group rejected, before turning to the EAC and SADC, which deployed troops and launched other initiatives.
He added, “The time came for the EAC and SADC to come together, but Tshisekedi placed Rwanda at the center of the issue, arguing that the problem was not AFC/M23 but Rwanda. This led to two tracks: the AFC/M23 talks in Nairobi and the Rwanda-DRC talks in Luanda, which were later handed over to the AU.”
According to Prof. Tombola, the United States and Qatar later joined the process, culminating in the Washington Agreement, but he said the DRC has implemented it only partially.
“In all this, you wonder whether those who sit at the table truly ignore the problem,” he said. “Is it necessary to move from city to city when the issue is already well known and no decisions are being implemented?”
He argued that the DRC continues to disregard agreements reached in Nairobi, Luanda, and Washington, adding that had they been respected, the crisis would have been resolved. He therefore described the Lomé initiative as “another Tshisekedi maneuver.”
“Tshisekedi is not implementing what was agreed in Washington and Doha, but is instead launching another process to keep people busy,” he said. “It is not because he believes Lomé will bring a solution, but because he is delaying what needs to be implemented.”
Meanwhile, Rwandan Minister of Foreign Affairs Olivier Nduhungirehe stated that peace talks in the Great Lakes Region should build on the steps taken in 2025, when the Rwanda-DRC agreement was signed in Washington.

title: Central African Republic Court Confirms Touadéra’s Presidential Victory
excerpt: Bangui, Central African Republic - January 20, 2026 - The Constitutional Court of the Central African Republic (CAR) has officially confirmed the victory of President Faustin-Archange Touadéra in the December 28, 2025 presidential election. The elections were held alongside votes
title_en: Central African Republic Court Confirms Touadéra’s Presidential Victory
excerpt_en: Bangui, Central African Republic - January 20, 2026 - The Constitutional Court of the Central African Republic (CAR) has officially confirmed the victory of President Faustin-Archange Touadéra in the December 28, 2025 presidential election. The elections were held alongside votes
body_en:
Bangui, Central African Republic - January 20, 2026 - The Constitutional Court of the Central African Republic (CAR) has officially confirmed the victory of President Faustin-Archange Touadéra in the December 28, 2025 presidential election. The elections were held alongside votes for the National Assembly and local authorities, with the electoral commission reporting a 52.42% turnout of more than 2.3 million registered voters.
Two weeks prior, the commission had announced that Touadéra won with 76.15% of the vote, defeating seven other candidates, including Anicet-Georges Dologuélé, who received 13.5% and petitioned the court to annul the results, alleging fraud.
On January 19, 2026, the court declared Touadéra the winner with 77.9% of the vote, dismissing Dologuélé’s challenge.
President Touadéra, in power since 2016, is eligible for a third term following a constitutional revision in 2023.
After the court’s confirmation, Touadéra told reporters he would focus on furthering peace, security, and good governance, while improving infrastructure for the population. He acknowledged progress in his administration’s first two terms but noted that gaps remain to be addressed in his third term.

excerpt: Moscow - January 21, 2026 - Russia has expressed skepticism that the ongoing conflict between Rwanda and the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) can be resolved without addressing its underlying causes, according to Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov. The Rwanda-DRC peace and economic
title_en: Russia Warns Rwanda-DRC Conflict Won’t End Without Addressing Root Causes
excerpt_en: Moscow - January 21, 2026 - Russia has expressed skepticism that the ongoing conflict between Rwanda and the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) can be resolved without addressing its underlying causes, according to Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov. The Rwanda-DRC peace and economic
body_en:
Moscow - January 21, 2026 - Russia has expressed skepticism that the ongoing conflict between Rwanda and the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) can be resolved without addressing its underlying causes, according to Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov.
The Rwanda-DRC peace and economic cooperation agreement, signed on December 4, 2025 with U.S. support, aims to resolve the conflict if fully implemented. The agreement specifically calls for dismantling the FDLR terrorist group, active in eastern DRC for years, which both countries agree poses a critical threat.
Lavrov noted that although the DRC government pledged to dismantle the FDLR by June 2025, it has yet to act, continuing to supply the group with weapons, food, and money while supporting the AFC/M23 coalition.
Speaking at a press conference in Moscow on January 20, 2026, Lavrov stated that Russia sees no signs of imminent resolution. He emphasized that the conflict cannot be resolved without tackling its known root causes and acknowledged the influence of the M23 armed group, which, despite lacking legal recognition in the DRC, wields significant power.
Lavrov affirmed that Russia maintains good relations with both Rwanda and the DRC and is prepared to provide assistance if requested to help resolve the conflict quickly.

title: Minister Nduhungirehe Calls for Africa-Europe Cooperation Based on Mutual Respect
excerpt: Davos, January 22, 2026 - Rwanda’s Minister of Foreign Affairs, Olivier Nduhungirehe, stressed the need for Africa and Europe to base their partnership on mutual respect rather than the legacy of colonialism, during a Leaders Forum held as part of the World Economic Forum in Davo
title_en: Minister Nduhungirehe Calls for Africa-Europe Cooperation Based on Mutual Respect
excerpt_en: Davos, January 22, 2026 - Rwanda’s Minister of Foreign Affairs, Olivier Nduhungirehe, stressed the need for Africa and Europe to base their partnership on mutual respect rather than the legacy of colonialism, during a Leaders Forum held as part of the World Economic Forum in Davo
body_en:
Davos, January 22, 2026 - Rwanda’s Minister of Foreign Affairs, Olivier Nduhungirehe, stressed the need for Africa and Europe to base their partnership on mutual respect rather than the legacy of colonialism, during a Leaders Forum held as part of the World Economic Forum in Davos, Switzerland.
Nduhungirehe highlighted Europe’s continuing economic strength and importance as a development partner while emphasizing that African nations should move beyond aid-driven relationships toward trade-based cooperation and investment partnerships. He cited Rwanda’s ongoing engagement with the European Union, including a €95 million grant in October 2025 to support vaccine production.
Europe and the Legacy of the Genocide
Addressing Europe’s historical role, Minister Nduhungirehe recalled the continent’s involvement in the 1994 Genocide against the Tutsi, which claimed over a million lives. He pointed to the actions of several European countries:
Belgium for fostering divisions during the colonial era.
France for abandoning Tutsi victims and facilitating the escape of perpetrators.
Other countries that served as refuges for genocide perpetrators.
“Some causes of the genocide stem from the colonial era. Racial discrimination by colonialists left deep scars. Today, Rwanda pursues unity and reconciliation, justice has been served, and we live together in one country,” Nduhungirehe said.
He also highlighted Rwanda’s economic recovery and development, with a focus on trade, investment, and human capital.
Africa’s Growing Role in Global Affairs
On Africa’s role in world governance, Nduhungirehe noted that since the UN’s establishment post-World War II, the continent had little influence. But today, Africa’s population of 1.4 billion, dominated by youth, positions it as a key player on the global stage. He emphasized collaboration with the US, EU, Russia, and China, particularly in modern technologies such as artificial intelligence.
“Africa has natural resources and a young population. With cooperation, finance, and knowledge sharing, we can build a skilled workforce for the future,” he said.
Rwanda-Poland Cooperation as a Model
Nduhungirehe also highlighted Rwanda’s strong partnership with Poland, noting agreements on trade, green technology, education, and security. Both countries have opened embassies in each other’s capitals, and over 1,500 Rwandans currently study in Poland, the largest foreign student group from a single country.
He cited the LuNa Smelter, a Rwandan tin processing plant supported by Polish investment, as an example of effective industrial cooperation.
Looking Forward
Minister Nduhungirehe concluded that Africa-Europe relations must evolve into mutually respectful partnerships, leveraging Africa’s investment potential while addressing internal challenges such as corruption, governance gaps, and youth inclusion.
“Africa has much to offer, but Africans must also take responsibility for their own development,” he said.

title: US Congressman Advocates Regional Sharing of Eastern DRC Mineral Wealth
excerpt: Washington, January 23, 2026 - Representative Ronny Jackson, a member of the United States House Foreign Affairs Committee, called for regional cooperation in managing minerals from eastern Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), arguing that neighboring countries should share in the
title_en: US Congressman Advocates Regional Sharing of Eastern DRC Mineral Wealth
excerpt_en: Washington, January 23, 2026 - Representative Ronny Jackson, a member of the United States House Foreign Affairs Committee, called for regional cooperation in managing minerals from eastern Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), arguing that neighboring countries should share in the
body_en:
Washington, January 23, 2026 - Representative Ronny Jackson, a member of the United States House Foreign Affairs Committee, called for regional cooperation in managing minerals from eastern Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), arguing that neighboring countries should share in the benefits to promote stability and security.
Jackson, who visited Rwanda, Burundi, Uganda, and other regional countries in 2025 to investigate the roots of the conflict between Rwanda and the DRC, presented his findings to US lawmakers on January 22, 2026.
“I have repeatedly suggested that there should be an agreement between countries-not only Rwanda, but also Burundi, Uganda, and other neighbors-so that everyone can benefit from the thousands of billions of dollars from minerals in eastern DRC,” Jackson said.
The congressman emphasized that processing the minerals in neighboring countries could foster shared responsibility for regional security.
“If these minerals are mined in the DRC and processed in neighboring countries, everyone will have an interest in maintaining peace in the region,” he explained.
Jackson also highlighted the importance of investing the revenue from these resources in eastern DRC to improve infrastructure, enhance living standards, and support local communities, framing economic development as a key factor in long-term stability.
His comments come amid ongoing tensions in eastern DRC, where armed groups, including the AFC/M23 coalition, have repeatedly clashed with government forces, and control of mineral-rich areas remains contested.

title: I&M Bank Partners with Toyota Rwanda to Expand Access to Vehicle Ownership
excerpt: Kigali, January 8, 2026 - I&M Bank Rwanda has entered into a strategic partnership with Toyota Rwanda Ltd to help customers acquire vehicles through affordable financing and exclusive price concessions. The partnership agreement was signed on January 8, 2026, at Toyota Rwanda’s h
title_en: I&M Bank Partners with Toyota Rwanda to Expand Access to Vehicle Ownership
excerpt_en: Kigali, January 8, 2026 - I&M Bank Rwanda has entered into a strategic partnership with Toyota Rwanda Ltd to help customers acquire vehicles through affordable financing and exclusive price concessions. The partnership agreement was signed on January 8, 2026, at Toyota Rwanda’s h
body_en:
Kigali, January 8, 2026 - I&M Bank Rwanda has entered into a strategic partnership with Toyota Rwanda Ltd to help customers acquire vehicles through affordable financing and exclusive price concessions.
The partnership agreement was signed on January 8, 2026, at Toyota Rwanda’s headquarters in Karuruma, Kigali City. Toyota Rwanda is the authorized distributor of Toyota vehicles and accessories in the country.
Under the agreement, I&M Bank customers - as well as prospective clients - will be able to purchase Toyota vehicles through soft loans and preferential pricing, making car ownership more accessible, particularly for individuals with limited financial resources.
Speaking at the signing ceremony, the Head of Retail Banking and Branches at I&M Bank Rwanda, Yves Kayihura, said the initiative aims to remove financial barriers and promote broader access to reliable transportation.
“This partnership will enable our customers to access quality vehicles while the bank uses the car itself as collateral, eliminating the need for additional assets,” Kayihura said. “We are also providing insurance services, allowing customers to complete the entire process through one institution in a short time.”
He added that I&M Bank has a dedicated car lending department and an integrated insurance system to ensure a seamless customer experience.
Toyota Rwanda’s Chief Operating Officer, Patrick Kanyandekwe, said the agreement reflects the company’s commitment to improving customer service and strengthening its collaboration with financial institutions.
“This partnership will make it easier for customers to receive discounts on the vehicles they want and obtain them quickly,” Kanyandekwe said. “It also demonstrates our desire to continue enhancing our services while maintaining a strong relationship with I&M Bank.”
He further noted that Toyota Rwanda remains responsible for post-sale vehicle servicing and currently offers a range of 13 different vehicle models to meet diverse customer needs.
