title: Wazalendo Takes Control of Uvira After M23 Withdrawal
excerpt: Uvira, January 18, 2026 - Wazalendo fighters have begun taking control of Uvira town following the withdrawal of the AFC/M23 in compliance with ongoing peace talks in the Democratic Republic of Congo. Residents confirmed that Wazalendo forces entered the town on Sunday morning, a
title_en: Wazalendo Takes Control of Uvira After M23 Withdrawal
excerpt_en: Uvira, January 18, 2026 - Wazalendo fighters have begun taking control of Uvira town following the withdrawal of the AFC/M23 in compliance with ongoing peace talks in the Democratic Republic of Congo. Residents confirmed that Wazalendo forces entered the town on Sunday morning, a
body_en:
Uvira, January 18, 2026 - Wazalendo fighters have begun taking control of Uvira town following the withdrawal of the AFC/M23 in compliance with ongoing peace talks in the Democratic Republic of Congo.
Residents confirmed that Wazalendo forces entered the town on Sunday morning, a day after AFC/M23 announced it had fully withdrawn. Videos circulating online show fighters abusing civilians and looting property.
A former South Kivu commander, now based in Kalemie, confirmed the return of Wazalendo fighters, saying they were awaiting instructions from their superiors.
“We must be very careful. Our leaders must first verify that what M23 is saying is true,” he said.
Despite their presence, AFC/M23 stated that it had left Uvira under the responsibility of the international community, urging it to ensure the safety of residents.
In a letter dated January 15, 2026, AFC/M23 informed the United Nations Secretary-General that it had requested MONUSCO to protect the city’s population.
“Our organization, AFC/M23, has decided to place the city of Uvira under the full responsibility of the international community,” said Corneille Nangaa, leader of the group.
He added that a small AFC/M23 monitoring unit had remained temporarily in the town while awaiting the deployment of neutral forces, but that this unit also withdrew on January 15.
AFC/M23 warned the UN that the Burundian army, the FDLR terrorist group, Wazalendo groups, and the Cancuro pose serious security threats to Uvira’s residents.
“Their presence and activities not only threaten the security of civilians, but also the peace process and the security of the region,” the group said.
The coalition called for the urgent deployment of neutral forces to prevent a return to the violence experienced when the city was under DRC government control.
AFC/M23 captured Uvira on December 9, 2025, after a week-long battle in parts of the Ruzizi Valley in South Kivu Province. It said the withdrawal followed a request from the United States to allow peace talks to continue. The group was asked to return to positions within 75 kilometers of the city to enable the international community to ensure civilian protection.
Residents had reported a period of relative calm under M23 control, with people resuming daily activities without violence, theft, or looting.
However, concerns remain high, with fears that following the M23 withdrawal, supporters of the group could face reprisals or targeted killings.

title: Ndayishimiye Appeals to DRC for Support as Congolese Refugees Remain Blocked in Burundi
excerpt: January 18, 2026 - Burundian President Évariste Ndayishimiye has renewed his appeal to the Government of the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) for assistance in caring for Congolese refugees, saying Burundi lacks the capacity to support them after refusing to allow their return.
title_en: Ndayishimiye Appeals to DRC for Support as Congolese Refugees Remain Blocked in Burundi
excerpt_en: January 18, 2026 - Burundian President Évariste Ndayishimiye has renewed his appeal to the Government of the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) for assistance in caring for Congolese refugees, saying Burundi lacks the capacity to support them after refusing to allow their return.
body_en:
January 18, 2026 - Burundian President Évariste Ndayishimiye has renewed his appeal to the Government of the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) for assistance in caring for Congolese refugees, saying Burundi lacks the capacity to support them after refusing to allow their return.
The fighting between the AFC/M23 Alliance and the coalition of DRC government forces (FARDC), Wazalendo groups, Burundian troops, and the FDLR in South Kivu Province has forced thousands to flee into Burundi.
After parts of Uvira became safer, some refugees attempted to return home, but Burundi closed its borders and refused their return. Many refugees continue to endure harsh living conditions, with reports of deaths from disease linked to unsanitary camp conditions.
President Ndayishimiye said the DRC government should take responsibility for its citizens and provide assistance, stressing that they did not flee their government but rather armed attacks.
“I ask the DRC government to see how it can help them, because I do not consider them refugees but people who have moved from one place to another after fleeing the enemy, not their government,” he said.
He added, “This means the Congolese government has a responsibility to follow them and care for their health and well-being, because they are not enemies of the government.”
Ndayishimiye also called on the DRC to mobilize international organizations for humanitarian assistance, noting that Burundi does not have the necessary capacity to support the refugees alone.
“In Burundi, we are trying to mobilize the population to help these people, but in reality it is difficult. Burundi lacks the capacity, and we must work together,” he said.
In early December 2025, more than 100,000 refugees crossed into Burundi after fleeing clashes in parts of the Ruzizi Valley, joining others who had already been displaced.
Many of the newly arrived refugees, initially placed in temporary camps near the border, have repeatedly appealed to the Burundian government to allow them to return home, citing severe hardship and rising deaths.
Instead, authorities have begun relocating refugees to camps further inland, including Busuma in the former Ruyigi Province, where conditions remain extremely difficult, prompting protests demanding permission to return.

However, on the morning of January 18, Wazalendo rebels, including fighters led by Gen. Ngomanzito, entered the town and announced their intention to continue fighting to remove AFC/M23 forces from all areas under their control.
Since then, Wazalendo fighters, alongside some residents, have reportedly been looting homes, particularly those belonging to the Banyamulenge community and their churches, seizing equipment and property. Some reportedly declared they did not want Rwandans in the town.
Later that afternoon, DRC special forces were seen entering Uvira, with some soldiers arriving on foot and others in Jeeps.
The government-appointed Governor of South Kivu, Jean-Jacques Purusi, indicated that he may soon return from exile in Burundi to resume his duties in Uvira.
The Permanent Secretary of AFC/M23, Benjamin Mbonimpa, warned that if DRC government forces attack AFC/M23 positions, they will be defeated.
Responding to the government spokesperson, Mbonimpa said: “Your troops are returning to Uvira. What will happen is that they will attack our positions. What will also happen is that they will be defeated. What will not happen is that the diplomatic support you have been receiving until today will continue.”
Following their withdrawal, AFC/M23 fighters moved toward areas including Kamanyola. The United States had requested that they relocate to positions within 75 kilometers of Uvira.

body_en:
Kamanyola, DRC - January 19, 2026 - Members of the Banyamulenge community living in Uvira, South Kivu Province in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, have fled to Kamanyola Center in Walungu Territory following the withdrawal of AFC/M23 fighters from the town.
The leader of the Banyamulenge community in Uvira, Muyoboke Ndatabaye, announced on January 18 via the YouTube channel “Agasaro Kaburaga” that the decision was taken due to fears of reprisals from DRC government forces and Wazalendo groups.
According to Ndatabaye, after AFC/M23 announced it would evacuate its remaining fighters from Uvira, members of the Wazalendo militias began sending messages to Banyamulenge residents, threatening to kill them and accusing them of being Rwandans who did not belong in the country.
“On Friday, gangs began to form. You could see people scattered, appearing to organize to harm others. Then yesterday we held a meeting with the population, and I informed them that AFC/M23 had decided to leave the city,” he said.
He added, “After that, people said, ‘We can’t wait any longer for the Wazalendo to attack us,’ so we decided to flee.”
Ndatabaye reported that from the morning of January 18, Banyamulenge homes and their churches were attacked by Wazalendo fighters, with properties destroyed and looted. He confirmed that many families have already fled.
“We are now in Kamanyola. No one has crossed the border. Women, children, and men are sheltering at a school. Those who wish can come and see us. Here we feel safe, even though conditions are difficult. If the Wazalendo remain there, we will continue moving until we reach the border,” he said.
Ndatabaye stated that when AFC/M23 controlled Uvira, the Banyamulenge lived peacefully, noting that prior to that, their security had been threatened by Wazalendo groups. He added that they no longer feel able to coexist with militias they say are supported by the DRC government.

title: Why Soldiers and Youth Are Fleeing Burundi in Large Numbers
excerpt: Bujumbura, January 19, 2026 - Burundi, one of the world’s poorest countries, appears to have reached a breaking point, as growing numbers of soldiers and young people flee the country amid worsening economic hardship and political disillusionment. Although President Évariste Nday
title_en: Why Soldiers and Youth Are Fleeing Burundi in Large Numbers
excerpt_en: Bujumbura, January 19, 2026 - Burundi, one of the world’s poorest countries, appears to have reached a breaking point, as growing numbers of soldiers and young people flee the country amid worsening economic hardship and political disillusionment. Although President Évariste Nday
body_en:
Bujumbura, January 19, 2026 - Burundi, one of the world’s poorest countries, appears to have reached a breaking point, as growing numbers of soldiers and young people flee the country amid worsening economic hardship and political disillusionment.
Although President Évariste Ndayishimiye took office in June 2020 promising economic recovery, his administration has overseen a sharp deterioration in living conditions, with poverty levels now worse than during the last period of relative stability.
At the center of the crisis is an agreement with President Félix Tshisekedi to deploy Burundian troops to fight the AFC/M23 coalition in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC). The deployment has resulted in soldier casualties, prolonged salary delays, and widespread demoralization within the armed forces.
As a result, many soldiers have deserted, fleeing to countries such as Zambia, Mozambique, and even parts of Asia. The government has responded with tightened border controls and has imprisoned immigration officials accused of issuing passports to deserters.
Meanwhile, Burundian youth are leaving the country in growing numbers, citing lack of employment opportunities, which many say are reserved for members of the ruling CNDD-FDD party. Numerous students have dropped out of school, believing that education offers little value without political affiliation.
In early 2025, school dropout rates reportedly reached 70% in some regions. In the former Kayanza province, more than 4,500 students left school in just three months during the 2024-2025 academic year.
According to the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR), the number of Burundian refugees in Rwanda increased by 1,721 between 2024 and 2025. As of December 31, 2025, Rwanda was hosting 52,961 Burundian refugees, representing 38.5% of the total refugee population in the country.
Across cities such as Kigali, Kampala, and Nairobi, Burundian youth are now working as street vendors and small traders, sending remittances home that often exceed the salaries of government employees in Burundi.
One young Burundian vendor in Nairobi said he earns about 3,000 Kenyan shillings per month, equivalent to more than 150,000 Burundian francs (Fbu), which he sends to his family. “It is small, but it helps them survive,” he said.
Despite the exodus of soldiers and youth, President Ndayishimiye continues to publicly claim that no country is as rich or blessed as Burundi - a statement many critics see as evidence of the regime’s disconnect from the daily struggles of its citizens.
The growing flight of human capital, observers warn, threatens to further undermine Burundi’s social stability and economic future.

title: Tensions Escalate in Uganda as Gen. Muhoozi Targets Bobi Wine
excerpt: Kampala, Uganda - January 20, 2026 - Political tensions in Uganda have intensified following statements by Army Chief of Staff Gen. Muhoozi Kainerugaba, who announced that 22 members of the National Unity Platform (NUP) were killed in a single week and appeared to threaten opposi
title_en: Tensions Escalate in Uganda as Gen. Muhoozi Targets Bobi Wine
excerpt_en: Kampala, Uganda - January 20, 2026 - Political tensions in Uganda have intensified following statements by Army Chief of Staff Gen. Muhoozi Kainerugaba, who announced that 22 members of the National Unity Platform (NUP) were killed in a single week and appeared to threaten opposi
body_en:
Kampala, Uganda - January 20, 2026 - Political tensions in Uganda have intensified following statements by Army Chief of Staff Gen. Muhoozi Kainerugaba, who announced that 22 members of the National Unity Platform (NUP) were killed in a single week and appeared to threaten opposition leader Bobi Wine, the popular name of Robert Kyagulanyi.
The conflict has deep roots, but political hostilities had largely subsided during the recent campaign period.
On January 15, during the Ugandan general elections, Bobi Wine, who secured 24.7% of the vote, second to President Yoweri Museveni, reported that his home was attacked by soldiers and police, forcing him to go into hiding.
That night, Ugandan authorities said that opposition supporters attempted to force their way into a vote counting center, resulting in more than 10 people killed.
Gen. Muhoozi issued several statements online threatening NUP members. In one post, he declared, “We have killed 22 NUP terrorists. I pray that the 23rd will be Bobi Wine.” He warned that opposition figures would be targeted wherever found unless President Museveni intervened.
He also reportedly gave Bobi Wine 48 hours to surrender to authorities, warning that failure to do so would result in him being treated as a rebel.
Responding to the threats, Bobi Wine stated that he had secured a safe location and would reveal himself on his own terms, criticizing the regime for attacking his home. He said: “You ordered an attack on my house to harm me; I defeated them, and they escaped. I will show myself when I want, and then you and your father can do whatever you want.”
The situation has sparked widespread concern, as some of Gen. Muhoozi’s messages included graphic threats against the opposition leader.
Following the elections, Bobi Wine and NUP party members denounced the provisional results, alleging they were rigged.
President Museveni was declared the winner, securing a seventh term with 71.6% of the vote, further fueling tensions between the ruling party and opposition forces.

title: Burundi Reinforces Military Presence in Kalemie Amid Tensions in Eastern DRC
excerpt: Kalemie, DRC - January 20, 2026 - Burundi has significantly increased its military presence in the town of Kalemie, capital of Tanganyika Province, amid concerns that the AFC/M23 coalition could resume fighting in the eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC). According to s
title_en: Burundi Reinforces Military Presence in Kalemie Amid Tensions in Eastern DRC
excerpt_en: Kalemie, DRC - January 20, 2026 - Burundi has significantly increased its military presence in the town of Kalemie, capital of Tanganyika Province, amid concerns that the AFC/M23 coalition could resume fighting in the eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC). According to s
body_en:
Kalemie, DRC - January 20, 2026 - Burundi has significantly increased its military presence in the town of Kalemie, capital of Tanganyika Province, amid concerns that the AFC/M23 coalition could resume fighting in the eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC).
According to security sources, the Burundian government has deployed up to 29,000 soldiers, along with members of the Imbonerakure, to protect the city from a possible takeover by AFC/M23 forces. In Kalemie, Burundian troops have reportedly coordinated with the DRC army, Wazalendo militias, the FDLR, as well as foreign contractors and personnel.
On January 13, two ships carrying hundreds of Burundian soldiers arrived at the Port of Kalemie from Bujumbura via Rumonge, according to eyewitnesses. Three days earlier, two aircraft had transported approximately 400 DRC soldiers into the city.
Analysts note that the current troop buildup resembles the situation in Goma at the end of 2024, when more than 60,000 troops were deployed to prevent AFC/M23 from capturing the city-an effort that ultimately failed when Goma fell on January 27, 2025.
In Kalemie, however, there is currently no confirmed evidence that AFC/M23 intends to advance on the city. The group previously captured Uvira on December 9, 2025, before withdrawing all fighters by January 17, 2026, moving toward Kamanyola.
The joint actions of the Burundian army, DRC forces, and allied groups suggest preparations for renewed military operations against AFC/M23 positions in South Kivu Province.
Sources in South Kivu report that since January 7, Burundian and DRC forces have been conducting surveillance operations on Lake Tanganyika, primarily from Kalemie, extending to Baraka and Makobola in Fizi Territory.
On that date, approximately 2,000 troops arrived aboard three ships at the Port of Baraka. Both in Baraka and Kalemie, heavy and light weapons, as well as other military equipment, have continued to be delivered.
The DRC government’s arsenal reportedly includes five surveillance drones, four CH-4 combat drones, two Sukhoi-25 fighter jets, three Mi-24 attack helicopters, and four Mi-8 transport helicopters, operated in part by foreign contractors.
On January 9, a boat carrying more than 150 Burundian commandos, reportedly in disguise, was spotted at the Port of Baraka en route to Makobola. A Burundian soldier with the rank of sergeant said their mission was to attack AFC/M23 positions.
Leaders of Wazalendo militias, including William Yakutumba, who styles himself as “General,” also confirmed their intention to launch operations aimed at removing AFC/M23 from eastern DRC following its withdrawal from Uvira.
On January 18, the Permanent Secretary of AFC/M23, Benjamin Mbonimpa, warned that if DRC government forces continued to attack their positions, they would be defeated, adding that international support for the government would not be unconditional.

excerpt_en: Uvira, DRC - January 21, 2026 - The AFC/M23 coalition, which has been fighting the DRC government, explained the reasons behind its withdrawal from Uvira town before the arrival of neutral forces. Spokesperson Lawrence Kanyuka told researcher Dr. Bojana Coulibaly that the coaliti
body_en:
Uvira, DRC - January 21, 2026 - The AFC/M23 coalition, which has been fighting the DRC government, explained the reasons behind its withdrawal from Uvira town before the arrival of neutral forces.
Spokesperson Lawrence Kanyuka told researcher Dr. Bojana Coulibaly that the coalition had planned to leave a monitoring group in the city to maintain security, but mediators refused, demanding a full withdrawal. “There was politics behind it. We explained that we were not leaving Uvira to abandon residents, but they did not allow our group to stay,” Kanyuka said.
The coalition emphasized that it complied with all requirements, taking serious measures to ensure safety, and dissociated itself from any violence that occurred after its departure. Kanyuka expressed regret over atrocities committed by Wazalendo groups and DRC forces, including looting, destruction of homes and churches, and torture since January 18, 2026.
The withdrawal plan had initially been announced on December 16, 2025, with the coalition leaving by January 17, 2026, after waiting for the neutral forces to arrive.

excerpt_en: Uvira, DRC - January 21, 2026 - More than 1,000 Congolese Tutsi fled Uvira town after the AFC/M23 coalition withdrew its fighters. A local civil society member reported that between January 19 and 20, FDLR, DRC, and Wazalendo forces abducted residents and took them to unknown loc
body_en:
Uvira, DRC - January 21, 2026 - More than 1,000 Congolese Tutsi fled Uvira town after the AFC/M23 coalition withdrew its fighters.
A local civil society member reported that between January 19 and 20, FDLR, DRC, and Wazalendo forces abducted residents and took them to unknown locations.
Over 300 Tutsi families sought refuge in the Kamanyola Center in Walungu Territory, under AFC/M23 control. Spokesperson Lawrence Kanyuka added that more than 200 Banyamulenge families relocated from Kamanyola Town.
Attempts by some residents to reach the highlands connecting Uvira, Fizi, and Mwenga Territories were blocked by Wazalendo fighters. While those in Kamanyola are reportedly safe, many remain worried for relatives still in Uvira.

title_en: Two Arrested for Bribery and Selling Substandard Alcohol
excerpt_en: Ruhango, Rwanda - January 21, 2026 - The Rwanda National Police (RNP) arrested a 56-year-old man and a 65-year-old woman on suspicion of bribing security forces with 50,000 Rwf. The suspects were caught distilling and selling 780 liters of substandard alcohol known as Igikwangari
body_en:
Ruhango, Rwanda - January 21, 2026 - The Rwanda National Police (RNP) arrested a 56-year-old man and a 65-year-old woman on suspicion of bribing security forces with 50,000 Rwf.
The suspects were caught distilling and selling 780 liters of substandard alcohol known as Igikwangari. The operation, carried out by local authorities and the public, led to the immediate destruction of the liquor.
CIP Kamanzi Hassan, police spokesperson for the Southern Province, confirmed that the individuals are detained at Byimana Police Station and that the Judicial Police have begun investigations.
He reminded citizens that giving or receiving bribes and producing or selling substandard alcohol are criminal offenses and urged the public to report crimes promptly to prevent harm to communities.

title: AFC/M23 Leader Says Withdrawal from Uvira Aimed at Supporting Peace Talks
excerpt: Bukavu DRC, January 22, 2026 - During a meeting of AFC/M23 members in Bukavu on January 21, leader Corneille Nangaa explained that the rebel group’s decision to withdraw from Uvira was made to demonstrate willingness for peace talks. Nangaa stated that while AFC/M23 previously ca

excerpt_en: Bukavu DRC, January 22, 2026 - During a meeting of AFC/M23 members in Bukavu on January 21, leader Corneille Nangaa explained that the rebel group’s decision to withdraw from Uvira was made to demonstrate willingness for peace talks. Nangaa stated that while AFC/M23 previously ca
body_en:
Bukavu DRC, January 22, 2026 - During a meeting of AFC/M23 members in Bukavu on January 21, leader Corneille Nangaa explained that the rebel group’s decision to withdraw from Uvira was made to demonstrate willingness for peace talks.
Nangaa stated that while AFC/M23 previously captured Uvira, the withdrawal was intended to build trust in ongoing negotiations.
“In recent days you’ve heard calls for ‘Uvira, Uvira, Uvira.’ We left Uvira to show goodwill, as we have been repeatedly asked to vacate the city, demonstrating that AFC/M23 does not seek war,” Nangaa said.
He emphasized that the group maintains capable forces, noting that the decision to return to Uvira was operationally feasible, but not the ultimate goal.
“There is no doubt you have forces. Today we say we could go back to Uvira if needed. We have all the capabilities, but that is not our objective,” Nangaa added.
The rebels entered Uvira on December 9, 2025. A week later, the group announced it would withdraw at the request of the United States, which assured the continuation of peace talks. By January 17, 2026, AFC/M23 had partially left the city, awaiting the arrival of neutral forces, after which Congolese troops and Wazalendo militias re-entered Uvira.

title: Five RDF Officers Graduate from Four-Year Military Training in Qatar
excerpt: Qatar, January 22, 2026 - Five junior officers of the Rwandan Defence Forces (RDF) successfully completed a four-year training program at various military schools in Qatar, in a ceremony attended by Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad Al-Thani, Emir of Qatar. Representing the RDF, Col. Bernar
title_en: Five RDF Officers Graduate from Four-Year Military Training in Qatar
excerpt_en: Qatar, January 22, 2026 - Five junior officers of the Rwandan Defence Forces (RDF) successfully completed a four-year training program at various military schools in Qatar, in a ceremony attended by Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad Al-Thani, Emir of Qatar. Representing the RDF, Col. Bernar
body_en:
Qatar, January 22, 2026 - Five junior officers of the Rwandan Defence Forces (RDF) successfully completed a four-year training program at various military schools in Qatar, in a ceremony attended by Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad Al-Thani, Emir of Qatar.
Representing the RDF, Col. Bernard Niyomugabo, Defence Attaché at the Rwandan Embassy in Qatar, praised the officers’ dedication and highlighted the importance of the training for enhancing Rwanda’s military capabilities.
This milestone continues a long-standing partnership between Rwanda and Qatar in defense and security cooperation. In January 2025, nine RDF soldiers completed similar training programs in Qatar, demonstrating the ongoing commitment of both countries to strengthen military skills and safeguard national sovereignty.
The ceremony was also attended by Rwandan officials, including Brig. Gen. Franco Rutagengwa, Director of the Gako Military Academy, who emphasized the strategic significance of international military training in preparing Rwanda’s officers for modern security challenges.
Broader Rwanda-Qatar Cooperation
Military training is just one aspect of the growing partnership between Rwanda and Qatar. The two countries have collaborated in several sectors, including:
Security: At the end of 2024, the Rwandan Police and the Qatari Internal Security Service signed a cooperation agreement on security and crime prevention.
Air Transport: Qatar Airways is expected to acquire a 49% stake in RwandAir, while Qatar holds a 60% share in the Bugesera Airport project, which is designed to handle 14 million passengers per year upon completion.
Investment and Strategic Cooperation: The partnership spans multiple sectors, reflecting strong diplomatic ties between Kigali and Doha.
“Training in Qatar equips our officers with advanced skills, enabling them to protect Rwanda’s sovereignty effectively,” Col. Niyomugabo said.
This latest graduation underscores the strengthening bilateral relations and Rwanda’s commitment to professionalizing its armed forces through international partnerships.

title: Security Measures to Remain Until FDLR Dismantled, Ambassador Tells US Lawmakers
excerpt: Washington, January 22, 2026 - Rwanda has reaffirmed that its security measures will remain in effect until the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) dismantles the FDLR terrorist group, according to a statement by Rwandan Ambassador to the United States, Mathilde Mukantabana, befor
title_en: Security Measures to Remain Until FDLR Dismantled, Ambassador Tells US Lawmakers
excerpt_en: Washington, January 22, 2026 - Rwanda has reaffirmed that its security measures will remain in effect until the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) dismantles the FDLR terrorist group, according to a statement by Rwandan Ambassador to the United States, Mathilde Mukantabana, befor
body_en:
Washington, January 22, 2026 - Rwanda has reaffirmed that its security measures will remain in effect until the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) dismantles the FDLR terrorist group, according to a statement by Rwandan Ambassador to the United States, Mathilde Mukantabana, before the US House of Representatives Subcommittee on Foreign Affairs.
Addressing lawmakers responsible for monitoring developments in Africa, Ambassador Mukantabana traced the origins of the FDLR, noting that its members have committed crimes for over 31 years. She highlighted that the US State Department designated the ALiR/FDLR as a terrorist organization in 2001 following attacks on tourists, including Americans, in Uganda's Bwindi Impenetrable National Park in May 1999.
“Today, the FDLR remains active in eastern DRC, integrated into the operations of the DRC military. UN experts continue to document its activities. This genocidal group, which has existed since 1994, has not been defeated, has been preserved, protected, and supported by successive DRC governments,” Ambassador Mukantabana said.
The ambassador stressed that the DRC’s cooperation with the FDLR, particularly in military operations against the AFC/M23, poses a direct threat to Rwanda. She cited a recent incident in late January 2025, when the group bombed the town of Rubavu, only to be repelled by Rwandan forces.
“Our operations are solely aimed at protecting the Rwandan population by preventing cross-border threats. These measures are not related to seeking political advantage in the DRC or supporting any specific group,” she explained.
Ambassador Mukantabana underlined that Rwanda’s security measures are temporary and will be lifted once the DRC complies with its obligations under the Washington Accords signed on June 27, 2025, and ratified on December 4, 2025. These accords require the DRC to dismantle the FDLR and repatriate its fighters.
“Rwanda’s security measures will be reviewed as the level of threat decreases. Once a review confirms that the DRC government has acted to dismantle the FDLR, these measures will be lifted,” the ambassador assured US lawmakers.
The statement reinforces Rwanda’s long-standing position that cross-border threats from armed groups in eastern DRC directly impact regional security and that responsibility lies with the DRC to neutralize such threats.

“Our operations are solely aimed at protecting the Rwandan population by preventing cross-border threats. These measures are not related to seeking political advantage in the DRC or supporting any specific group,” she explained.
Ambassador Mukantabana underlined that Rwanda’s security measures are temporary and will be lifted once the DRC complies with its obligations under the Washington Accords signed on June 27, 2025, and ratified on December 4, 2025. These accords require the DRC to dismantle the FDLR and repatriate its fighters.
“Rwanda’s security measures will be reviewed as the level of threat decreases. Once a review confirms that the DRC government has acted to dismantle the FDLR, these measures will be lifted,” the ambassador assured US lawmakers.
The statement reinforces Rwanda’s long-standing position that cross-border threats from armed groups in eastern DRC directly impact regional security and that responsibility lies with the DRC to neutralize such threats.

title: US Urges DRC to Stop FDLR Operations in Eastern Congo

title_en: US Urges DRC to Stop FDLR Operations in Eastern Congo
excerpt_en: Washington, January 22, 2026 - Senior US State Department officials have called on the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) to prevent the FDLR terrorist group from operating in its eastern provinces, citing ongoing security risks for Rwanda and the region. Sarah Troutman, a senior
body_en:
Washington, January 22, 2026 - Senior US State Department officials have called on the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) to prevent the FDLR terrorist group from operating in its eastern provinces, citing ongoing security risks for Rwanda and the region.
Sarah Troutman, a senior US official overseeing African affairs, told lawmakers that the FDLR, responsible for multiple attacks and linked to the 1994 Rwandan genocide, must not be allowed to operate in eastern DRC.
“The FDLR is a proven problem. It should not be allowed to operate in eastern DRC,” Troutman said during a session of US lawmakers monitoring developments in Africa.
The remarks came amid concerns that the DRC army continues to cooperate with the FDLR, in violation of the Washington-brokered peace agreement signed on June 27, 2025, which called for the group’s dismantling and for the removal of Rwandan security measures along the border.
US Representative Sarah Jacobs noted:
“On the part of the DRC army, they are said to continue working with the FDLR, a group founded by the organizers of the Genocide in Rwanda in 1994, in violation of the peace agreement.”
Rwandan Ambassador to the United States, Mathilde Mukantabana, reiterated that Rwanda’s security measures remain in place because the FDLR continues to receive support from elements within the DRC and poses a direct threat to Rwandan security.
The Washington Accords require the DRC to dismantle the FDLR and repatriate its fighters. However, recent reports indicate ongoing support to the group. On November 28, 2025, the DRC reportedly sent the FDLR and allied groups three tons of ammunition and three tons of food, followed by additional ammunition on January 14, 2026, allegedly to fight against the AFC/M23 rebel group.
Troutman emphasized that the dismantling of the FDLR is critical to regional stability and urged the DRC government to take “concrete steps” to comply with its commitments.
“We remind the DRC government that dismantling the FDLR as agreed is very important, and we want to see more concrete steps taken,” she said.
The continued presence and support of the FDLR in eastern DRC underscore the fragile security situation and highlight the challenges facing the implementation of the Washington peace agreement.

title: DRC President Tshisekedi Signals Offensive to Retake Areas Controlled by AFC/M23
excerpt: Uvira, South Kivu, January 23, 2026 - President Félix Tshisekedi Tshilombo of the Democratic Republic of Congo has announced plans to launch military operations aimed at regaining territories currently under the control of the AFC/M23 coalition, following their withdrawal from Uv
title_en: DRC President Tshisekedi Signals Offensive to Retake Areas Controlled by AFC/M23
excerpt_en: Uvira, South Kivu, January 23, 2026 - President Félix Tshisekedi Tshilombo of the Democratic Republic of Congo has announced plans to launch military operations aimed at regaining territories currently under the control of the AFC/M23 coalition, following their withdrawal from Uv
body_en:
Uvira, South Kivu, January 23, 2026 - President Félix Tshisekedi Tshilombo of the Democratic Republic of Congo has announced plans to launch military operations aimed at regaining territories currently under the control of the AFC/M23 coalition, following their withdrawal from Uvira earlier this month.
The announcement came via Governor Jean-Jacques Purusi, appointed by the DRC government for South Kivu Province, who returned to Uvira from exile in Burundi on January 23. Addressing residents, Governor Purusi said:
“The Head of State instructed me to announce that we will continue the fight. After Uvira, operations will move to Kamanyola, and then we will continue until Bukavu, Goma, Bunagana-everywhere under rebel control.”
The AFC/M23 coalition had previously withdrawn its fighters from Uvira on January 17, 2026, reportedly at the request of the United States, which promised to continue peace talks if the withdrawal was carried out.
Following the pullout, DRC government forces and allied Wazalendo militias reentered Uvira on January 18. Many residents, particularly from the Banyamulenge community, had fled the city during the rebel occupation, seeking temporary refuge in areas still influenced by AFC/M23, including Kamanyola.
The government’s statements indicate that military operations will continue to secure eastern DRC towns and assert control over strategic areas previously held by the rebellion.
Conclusion
In summary, the period from January 12 to 24, 2026, was marked by Rwanda’s dual focus on strengthening international partnerships and navigating the complex security landscape of the Great Lakes Region.
The following key themes emerge from our report:
Diplomatic and Economic Expansion: Rwanda actively broadened its global reach by signing four strategic agreements with Oman in technology and transport , discussing financial cooperation with Luxembourg , and reaffirming long-standing ties with Russia. Domestically, the launch of the "e-Bid" platform and new partnerships in the banking sector signaled a continued drive toward private sector modernization.
Regional Security and Conflict Resolution: The report highlights the ongoing volatility in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC). While Rwanda called for the fulfillment of the Washington Accords and the dismantling of the FDLR , experts and international observers like Russia expressed skepticism due to the DRC government's perceived failure to address root causes. The strategic withdrawal of AFC/M23 from Uvira and the subsequent entry of Wazalendo forces underscored the fragile nature of current peace efforts.
Internal Governance and Social Challenges: On the domestic front, Rwanda showcased significant human rights progress to the UN, reporting a 97% implementation rate of previous recommendations. However, the report also notes pressing internal issues, including a surge in poaching at Volcanoes National Park and urgent calls from leadership to address food insecurity through agricultural research.
Electoral Dynamics in Neighboring States: The successful monitoring of Uganda’s elections by an EAC mission led by Rwanda , and the confirmation of President Touadéra’s victory in the Central African Republic , reflect the broader regional trend of consolidating political leadership amidst varying degrees of opposition and controversy.
Overall, the report portrays a nation making significant strides in technology, diplomacy, and governance, while remaining deeply entwined in the persistent security challenges of its neighboring territories.
By Jeff Buleli
